The text continues, and I now come to the purpose of my intervention:
"Ms. Mailly is a Federal Conservative Member in the National Capital Region who has not supported the teachers." The text then states that the language teachers will be holding their demonstration on July 6, on the eve, then, of the day this press release was delivered to me-at 2 o'clock pm, at 300 Notre-Dame Street, Gatineau, at Claudy Mailly's riding office, and there follows a phone number where additional information could be obtained.
So I would like to submit this document. First, not only do I find it an act of intimidation directed at me, but they want me to intervene, Mr. Speaker, in a collective agreement and to take sides with one of the parties.
Second, Mr. Speaker, what is even more serious is that it is false. Not only did I support the teachers when they called me during this demonstration, but CHOT Television filmed and broadcast it. I supported the teachers then, not as an interven-or in the collective agreement, because I know that it is my duty not to intervene in such matters, but as a Member of Parliament, by telling them that I was going to speak on their behalf to the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) regarding their demands for preparation time and language of negotiations.
We were told that the negotiations were held entirely in English. So I interceded with the President of the Treasury Board. The Alliance was aware of this because I told the Alliance representative who was in my office. Television and radio reported these facts, but the weekly newspaper Le Dimanche Outaouais, of which I will table a copy, published a photo under which it says, "Demonstration at Claudy Mailly's Office: About thirty teachers of French as a second language working for the federal Government demonstrated in front of MP Claudy Mailly's office last Wednesday. Ms. Mailly is the only Member of Parliament who has not supported this group of 700 teachers who have been without a collective agreement for two years. The demonstrators gave 1,200 post cards of support from the people of Gatineau to Ms. Mailly's executive assistant in her absence." It does not mention at all that I spoke to them . . . Furthermore, I was away, Mr. Speaker, because I was in the House to vote on Bill C-72, which was really my duty as I saw it.
They took advantage of it, knowing very well that I fully supported Bill C-72, and that I would earn a reputation as a defender of French language rights. They chose that time to demonstrate in front of my office, without warning me. But despite that, I took the trouble to telephone the representative. They still distributed the erroneous communique and left it at my office.
Business of the House
I later wrote, Mr. Speaker, to the Public Service Alliance, to tell them that if they did not publicly apologize in a press release, because they knew they were wrong and admitted it, I would have to raise a question of privilege because I find it terrible that one would want to intimidate a Member of Parliament in the exercise of her duties in that way.
So I submit the case to you, Mr. Speaker, because I know that election fever is in the air and I would not want irresponsible journalists who do not check their sources to use what the Public Service Alliance has said with other unions, that they have blacklisted me to defeat me in my riding and that they have already begun to work at it. I find that is intimidation against me and besides, Mr. Speaker, if anyone defends francophones well, I do!

I just wanted that on the record. To blame the Government for not solving all the nation's problems in four years is a bit much. To ask whether the Government will refuse unanimous consent is to imply something that simply does not need dealing with. The Government does not intend to interfere with Private Members' Business. Mr. Speaker, my point is almost the same point as my hon. colleague. The NDP House Leader quoted me as saying in Maclean's magazine of July 18 something that I would have a hard time to explain. As usual, the NDP does not always read the whole article. However, I must confess this time that even if he had read it, it is not exactly what I said. Maclean's magazine did not report everything I said. What I said was: "No matter, $8 billion is a lot of cash. It is very hard to explain, but once you have the explanation that it is over a 25-year period and it is only $300 million a year, I have no problem at all. It is still a lot of cash but I have no problem at all to solve that. To update the fleet will cost more than that". I also said that at least 65 per cent of the project will be Canadian built and will create 55,000 person-years of work.
I just want to make it clear that the NDP did not quote me correctly and that Maclean's magazine did not quote the whole line. I have no problem in defending that. It is very easy to explain. It is too bad that my hon. colleague did not at least read the full line.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. de Cotret that Bill C-129, an Act to provide for the continuance of Air Canada under the Canada Business Corporations Act and for the issuance and sale of shares thereof to the public, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) had been recognized. Since he is not in the House I will recognize the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin).

Mr. Speaker, east or west, in the case of Regina the twain shall meet.
I am delighted to have an opportunity to attempt to persuade the Government to change its mind on legislation, the whole foundation of which is based on the worst kind of mythology. I want to deal with some of the specific points of the Government and those outside of Parliament who have attempted to justify the privatization of one of the best airlines in the world on grounds of business management. The five-year business plan of Air Canada itself shows why the legislation is unjustified, unnecessary, and a waste of taxpayers' money, the money of Canadian investors, and money which otherwise could have gone to Air Canada.
I will deal first with Air Canada's five-year business plan which takes it up to 1991 inclusive. Air Canada's business plan specifically excludes any privatization or the selling of shares to the general public. Air Canada specifically states that its five-year plan does not taken into account privatization. Air Canada's business plan says:
Profitability improves throughout the plan as does the debt/equity ratio because existing debt is retired and additional debt is not required. By 1990 the return on equity achieves the Corporate objective. Retained earnings grow steadily throughout the planning period.
That is without this Bill, Mr. Speaker. Air Canada has not changed its five-year plan since this Bill was brought in. Air

July 14, 1988
Air Canada
Canada is still operating on the basis of its five year business plan, which is without any privatization.
It has been stated repeatedly by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and the two previous Ministers that the purpose of privatization is to give Air Canada capital to buy new planes. That may be a valid position except that Air Canada, in its five-year plan, says:
-Air Canada will proceed with fleet renewal to take advantage of operating efficiencies available through new aircraft. The funds required for this multi-billion dollar investment will come largely from internally generated funds and borrowing. The airline's current drive to substantially increase earnings will therefore be maintained to generate the corporate share of the funds needed.
There is not a single word in Air Canada's own business plan about funds from the sale of shares.
It has been alleged by spokesmen from the government side, from outside this House, and from competing airlines, that Air Canada has the backing of the national Government, has access to government borrowings, et cetera.
My colleagues and good friends opposite forget that Air Canada itself says that it has received no equity infusion from the Government since 1977. That is 11 years ago. It says that it has received no government subsidies since 1962.
How does the Government explain its case that it is necessary to sell shares to the public in a company it already owns? That is another Barnum and Bailey con game if I ever saw one. As evidenced by Air Canada's own words, it does not need a nickel, has not received a nickel from the Government in equity since 1977, and has not received a nickel of subsidies since 1962.
Why do they want to be privatized?

My hon. friend asks why they want to be privatized. Mr. Jeanniot and Mr. Taylor of Air Canada are exactly the same as Mr. Lawless, the Chief Executive Officer of Canadian National who told the Transport Committee; "We'll take the capital money any way we can get it". I will explain to my hon. friend in a moment how Air Canada can and should be getting it. I will be happy to elucidate for my hon. friend.
The other reasons given for the legitimacy of privatizing Air Canada are better management, flexibility in management, and corporate decision making overnight without having to go to the Cabinet, Government, or Parliament of Canada. I raised this matter in the Transport Committee with officials of the Government, the Minister, and officials of Air Canada.
I asked whether Air Canada felt any restrictions on flexibility or management decisions in their daily and monthly operations. Air Canada said no. In fact, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), who I believe was a member of the Transport Committee at the time, will know that the Liberal Government in 1977 decided that Air Canada
should operate in a business-like fashion. According to the previous Government and the present Government, operating in a business-like fashion means one has to make a buck and not ask the Government for money. Air Canada has not asked for money, nor has it received any money.
When I asked that question in committee, the answer was no. It has not operated any differently than any other airline in this country. In fact, when Air Canada hears that Canadian Airlines International or Wardair holds a seat sale, Air Canada management has all the flexibility to announce the same fare or even a lower one overnight. When Air Canada announces a discount fare or seat sale, the other airlines can act overnight. There is absolutely no difference between any of the airlines in this country in terms of flexibility and management decisions. None of them conduct their affairs any differently, whether they are privately or publicly owned.
Therefore, the Government's argument for better management and flexibility is sheer nonsense. That argument falls on its face in front of the actual experience of Air Canada.
Air Canada has received international awards and gold medals as one of the best managed airlines in the world, but the Tories cannot stand that because it has the words "Crown corporation" in front of it. I would be quite happy to amend the Air Canada Act to eliminate the words "Crown corporation" if they would like. The point is, however, that it is a public utility that is owned and controlled by Canadians through its Parliament and its Government. That is the way it should be.
The Government and others in the private sector, particularly stockbrokers, have suggested that the public and employees can buy shares as a good investment in Air Canada. If it is a good investment, which it is, why would we not want the Government of Canada, on behalf of the taxpayers, to increase its investment?
It does not pay a dividend.

Exactly! My hon. friend has made my argument. In the last 11 years Air Canada showed net profits of $102.5 million, with $45 million last year and $40 million the year before. What did the shareholders in Canada get by way of a dividend? Not a nickel. The record speaks for itself. It has not paid any dividends. Surely the taxpayers of this country, as investors, are just as much entitled to an opportunity for a return on their investment as anyone who buys a share on the Toronto stockmarket or anywhere else that these gamblers operate. That is another nonsensical argument put forward by the Government as justification for selling to Canadians shares in something they already own.
The Government obviously intends to turn its social and economic responsibility for a national airline over to private interests so that it can continue to say, as the former Minister of Transport said, it will not interfere with the day-to-day operations and management decisions of the CNR or Air Canada. They want to place that responsibility with those in
July 14, 1988

the private sector so that the federal Government can avoid the responsibility for a national airline.
What are the costs of this privatization? I have been reading the figures about the brokerage fees and commissions when the British Government privatized several companies in that country. While I do not have anything to do with shares or the stockmarket, from what little I have been able to find out from some of those in the business, if 45 per cent of the shares of Air Canada are sold for $300 million the brokerage fees and commissions would come from that amount which Air Canada will receive. If the brokerage fees and commissions amount to $30 million on $300 million in share sales, Air Canada will get $270 million. That is somewhat short of what the Government claims it needs to buy new airplanes. In fact, Air Canada has said that it does not need that money to buy new airplanes.
Any net revenue taken in on the sale of shares will not be used to buy aircraft, it will be used to reduce the $2.3 billion debt of Air Canada, with assets in excess of that, in order to make it more attractive to sell off the rest of the company. This charade has gone on long enough. This is a corporation built and payed for by the taxpayers of Canada. They are entitled to a return on their investment but they are not getting it. The Government has put up nothing else but the wrong reasons for privatization. It is not to buy planes. It is to reduce debt. It is to reduce pressure on the Government.
The law already provides that the authorized capital for Air Canada is $750 million. The people of Canada in fact have less than half of that, $329 million, and the Government already has the authority to purchase additional share capital for Air Canada even to reduce debt or buy planes. It is already there.
This Bill is totally unnecessary. Its foundation is mythology. It is terrible when a democratic socialist has to teach Conservatives something about sound business practices. I hope the Government will have second thoughts and withdraw this Bill and not deal with it any further.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I thank all Hon. Members opposite who have stayed in the Chamber to hear my remarks with respect to this particular Bill. I particularly want to thank those Members from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island who obviously have a great interest in the subject matter and want to hear a viewpoint which is probably shared by them. Unfortunately, they have not found the courage nor, indeed, the conviction to stand up in the House of Commons and condemn what is best known in Atlantic Canada as a sell-off of a very important ingredient to the economy of Atlantic Canada.
The events surrounding Bill C-129 in coming to the House of Commons are indeed disturbing, not only to Members of
Air Canada
Parliament but to the general public and various interest groups across this country. The legislative committee on this particular Bill spent approximately one day contemplating its advantages and disadvantages.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), the official spokesperson for our Party, has demonstrated very clearly the position of our Party and why we are opposing this Bill. He has received numerous complaints from Canadians across this country who wanted that particular committee to review the Bill in detail and to hear their views on the importance of a nationally owned airline. Notwithstanding the substance contained in the McGrath report on parliamentary reform, the Government, which promised democracy, openness and fairness, has decided to say no to the commitments it made some time ago and to push through this Bill in a very quick fashion.
In addition to allowing only one day for the legislative committee, the Government refused Canadians in those regions of the country an opportunity to express their views in their own region. The committee did not travel to Atlantic Canada, western Canada, Ontario, Quebec or British Columbia. In fact to no part of this country did the committee travel.
Transport 2000 expressed it best when it said: "By selecting witnesses from exclusive airline management, organized labour and academic circles, the legislative committee overlooked Air Canada's most important constituency, the travelling public". How true that is. An airline conceived and implemented by a national government to service all the country is now in the hands of a Government which does not wish to hear the views of ordinary Canadians nor, indeed, those Canadians who use the airline the most. This is another example of a Government which is wedded to a concept of privatization notwithstanding the consequences. It is a blind and ill-conceived attitude on the Government's part.
Hon. Members opposite do not understand, nor do they appreciate, some of the institutions that a national government must put in place in order to sustain and enhance national unity and opportunities throughout the country. Partial privatization of this Crown corporation, I believe, will have negative effects on the various regions of this country. We have all heard Members opposite, as well as those on this side, speak glowingly and with a great deal of passion and concern in terms of trying to provide additional economic opportunities in their regions. We now have a Government which is backing off the very important clause contained in the Constitution, equality of opportunity. This legislation will, in the short run as well as in the long run, decrease the type of service we have in our regions. I speak primarily of my own region in Atlantic Canada. It will have an immediate as well as a long-term impact.
It is one thing for the Government to suggest that by selling 45 per cent of the shares, which value is yet to be determined, I am told, but taking the hypothetical figure of $300 million, it

July 14, 1988
Air Canada
is certainly not going to be sufficient to embark upon the purchase of new aircraft, which we are told may cost to the tune of $2 billion to $3 billion.
Air Canada will only want to have those routes which are exceptionally profitable. For example, flights from Halifax to Toronto are normally full to capacity. As a result, those flights, and those flights directly to Montreal, take place on a daily basis. They enable Air Canada as a Crown corporation to have a profitable margin on those flights so much so as to enable it to extend out into the hinterlands of the country to service such places as Corner Brook, Stephenville, Newfoundland, Yarmouth, Summerside, Charlottetown, Fredericton, Moncton and communities of that nature. Not all of the runs of Air Canada are lucrative enough to sustain its operations, so its most profitable operations such as the Halifax-Toronto run or the Halifax-Montreal run generate the needed revenues to provide the necessary, and I underline "necessary", service to the regions of this country.
One does not have to be a schoolteacher, a Philadelphia lawyer or a graduate of a business school to understand that those of us in the regions of the country, such as the region of Atlantic Canada, require the services of a national airline operating in our communities. Not only does a national airline provide service but it provides the necessary infrastructure which business, investment and the ordinary economic spinoffs need.
But what has the Government said to the regions of the country? It has said: "We are going to privatize Air Canada". Thereafter what will happen? You will see, Mr. Speaker, that the jet service into places such as Corner Brook, Newfoundland, Moncton, Fredericton and Sydney, which is in my own constituency, will be terminated. That will have an impact on economic developments in those communities. For what? The concept of privatization, a concept being espoused and expounded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski).
What is even more alarming is what the Prime Minister said on January 14, 1985. I do not want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, what my constituents think of this particular statement or the person who made it. The Prime Minister said: "Air Canada is not for sale. Canada needs a national airline. There is a possibility that shares in Air Canada will be sold to the public, but the Government would certainly retain a majority interest". I am not going to repeat, because I think it would be very unparliamentary, what my constituents were saying when I was in my constituency on the weekend. The language that they used is not, shall we say, very supportive. It is not very favourable to the Prime Minister or to the image of the Prime Minister and his Government.
On April 12, 1987, the Deputy Prime Minister, when he made a statement in the House of Commons, stated that the
legislation would permit the transfer of all Air Canada shares to the public, which is essentially the first phase. Once again, as we have seen from time to time in this Chamber, the Government says one thing and then does exactly the opposite. This is an affront to those regions of the country which do not share in the bounty and the wealth that the country has. The results will affect us and affect us negatively.
My colleague, our spokesperson, quite succinctly pointed out all the difficulties that we will have with regard to the privatization of Air Canada.
I just wish to underline for those Members who are in the Chamber and, indeed, for those Canadians who may be viewing this particular debate, that we said that, when it comes to regional economic development and when it comes to maximizing the opportunities for those of us who live in noneconomically viable communities, the erosion of Air Canada as we now know it will will result in the eventual lessening of service to those communities. It will happen sure as next year will be 1989. Governments are very much aware of that because they will cherry pick, the poor ones will be sold off to some other form of airline, which may or may not for a period of time use those runs for their purposes, and thereafter services will be terminated in their entirety to those various communities.
Air Canada was a symbol of national unity. It enhanced the feelings that we are one country, one nation, linked by our railroads, something which has since been terminated, and linked by an airline which the Government is trying to get away from. There are not only economic reasons why we in the Opposition are opposed to this measure, but there are other fundamental reasons as well.
There will be a reduction in the number of jobs as a result of this partial privatization. Earlier my colleague talked about the centralization of the reservations system. In fact, Air Canada's system in the United States is already centralized in New York. The day will come, and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not very far away-perhaps within the next fiscal year-when there will be nothing more than a centralization of reservations in the country, perhaps in Toronto or in Montreal.
What will happen to the rest of the country? There will be lay-offs in Moncton, which has already sustained more than its fair share of lay-offs with regard to the CN shops. There will be the lay-off of individuals at facilities such as those in Sydney and in Yarmouth. There will be lay-offs in Summer-side and in Charlottetown. There will be lay-offs as well in Newfoundland, in parts of Corner Brook and Stephenville. This privatization will certainly result in the loss of jobs as a result of the centralization of reservations.
Airline stewards may have to leave their families in order to locate in one central area, otherwise they may have to give up their high-paying jobs. Employees on feeder lines will no longer be unionized. Their wages could fall from $14 to less than $8 an hour. Fet us talk about that for a moment. That is
July 14, 1988

a very sizeable decrease in the wages that are paid to union members.
Those opposite ought to realize that it is the working person who is really the backbone of the Canadian economy. The more money one can pay an individual on an hourly rate, the more he or she can make a significant contribution. It is those people who have the surplus moneys to buy the durable goods, something that makes the economy go around. It is better to give to those producers and those workers than to lay it on in terms of corporate profits to Canadian banks or multinational pharmaceutical companies. That is where Canadians should be placing their dollars, which gives a true picture of a Canadian investing in his own country because of additional dollars.
Work will be contracted out. No longer will the services of many employees be needed. No assurances are coming forward with respect to how many employees will be retained in Winnipeg, although the legislation states that the maintenance base will not be closed. One would think that if one can give a commitment to keep the base open, then one can certainly give a commitment in terms of the number of employees who will be employed there. But, again, that identifies the hidden agenda of the Government.
We have heard many times before in this Chamber the Deputy Prime Minister say that there would be no lay-offs in Moncton when it came to CN. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), previously the Minister of Transport, stated to the communities of Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury that there would be no closure of their water plants, only to find that within a short period of time that was changed. There is no assurance that 500 employees at the financial branch located in Winnipeg will continue to be located there. The Government cannot give the community, the municipality, and the residents a clear legislative undertaking that that particular branch will remain in operation in Winnipeg. The Government is saying one thing, and on the other hand it does something that is entirely the opposite.
There will also be downgrading of services to less profitable routes, for example, Halifax to Sydney, frequency of flights versus the quality of the service, jets carrying disabled people, express freight, and industrial machinery.
There are a number of serious issues in those smaller runs. I mentioned the economics, but a great number of individuals travel from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Halifax in order to attend the Victoria General Hospital for proper medical care. Now they have to get on what we call little puddle-jumpers. This is inconvenient, difficult, and requires them to wait at wickets where there is no seating, if they are disabled, particularly in Halifax airport. Perhaps some Members are saying that that is not a major problem. It is a major problem when a substantial number of individuals and patients must go from one area of the province to another on a regular basis. By downgrading and doing away with the jet service once again we are hurting
Air Canada
those individuals who need the assistance of a Government, and of a caring Government.
There has been no opportunity for parliamentary scrutiny of the public share offering. The decision with respect to the value of Air Canada is being given carte blanche to investment dealers. Is it not nice that the investment dealers will get a bonanza of a return for their efforts? If it is $300 million, they will probably pick up $30 million. That is not a bad days pay for some of those investment brokers. Canadians have not had the opportunity to go forward and state their views as to what they believe to be the appropriate amount.
In conclusion, the privatization of Air Canada and the method the Government has chosen will be difficult for those of us who live in Atlantic Canada. The difficulties are compounded, because it will directly interfere with provincial, federal, and municipal Governments in their attempts to maximize and enhance economic opportunities. There will be a lessening of service to those communities that I have mentioned such as Sydney. There will be a major inconvenience to those in the travelling public, whether they are patients going to the Victoria General Hospital, or small business people who must travel to the capital city for a variety of reasons.
I hope that the Government in its conclusions and in reviewing what it has done will come to its senses and recognize the suggestions that have been made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLel-lan), who has been our official spokesperson and who has made numerous suggestions on how to enhance a situation which we believe could have a very serious and negative economic impact on our entire region.

I listened with interest to the Member in his participation in this debate, and I would like to raise a question that government Members have been putting as their reaction to speeches by the Opposition, and that is, the comment and the reality that Air Canada has not been the airline flying into the smaller communities, but that it has been one of the private sector airlines. Therefore, in the twisted logic of the Conservatives, they think that by privatizing Air Canada that will change.
From his experience in Atlantic Canada, could the Hon. Member indicate why Air Canada was not in there and aggressively providing that service? Was it because of the mandate of the Government of the day? Was it because there were private sector services there? How does the Hon. Member see that being affected by the change in Air Canada? Will we see Air Canada all of a sudden expand into those smaller communities, or will we see a situation where nothing changes?
What a loaded question.

It is becoming more and more apparent that questions of that nature, which are to the point and rather forthright in terms of their substance, have to be addressed by all Members. In communities in Atlantic Canada Air Canada

July 14, 1988
Air Canada
has provided the service. It has led the way and taken the initiative to provide service to those communities, both in terms of passenger and cargo service. Transportation and air transportation must be first and foremost a major part of any economic model. Because the Government of the day is urging Air Canada to get out of those smaller runs which do not generate the same profit as the big runs, for example, from Halifax to Toronto, or Halifax to Montreal, it is being given out to new airlines to pick up those routes.
A very good example of that has happened. A new company called Air Bras-d'Or, funded by the Government of Canada, opened its doors and advertised that it was going to transfer people from Sydney to Halifax to Port Hawkesbury. What happened to Air Bras-d'Or? There is no longer an Air Bras-d'Or company servicing that particular area, because it could not generate sustainable profits over a period of time to stay in existence. However, with a national airline reaping the profits from the major routes, it then had the ability and cash flow to service smaller communities.
I guess that the Government is only concerned with that corridor of Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver. I would have thought that representatives from Charlottetown would have been so concerned that they would have stood up for the people of Charlottetown after a Liberal Government put in place one of the nicest airports in all of Atlantic Canada. We will find within the next fiscal year that there will be lay-offs of employees at the Charlottetown airport, and we will find that the service will decrease substantially. We will also find that the economic benefits and opportunities will decrease accordingly because the Government has failed to keep a national airline serving all of Canada, not only the plush corridors of this country.
Charlottetown is a plush corridor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am motivated to make a few comments. This debate is deja vu. This is the thirteenth privatization of this Government, and I hear the same predictions about lay-offs from the same speakers. I hear the same predictions about drop in service from the same speakers. I challenge the Hon. Member to stand in his place and name one of our privatizations that has produced lay-offs rather than increased jobs, increased service, and increased customers. That is the characteristic of each and every privatization undertaken by the Government.
The same thing will happen with the privatization of Air Canada. The deregulation which this Government has accomplished has produced association between feeder airlines and the larger companies. Employees are better paid, more satisfied. There are more services to more communities through more flights. The safety record is outstanding.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reason is really quite simple. No company makes a profit without customers who pay the bills. In the airline business it is service, schedules, equipment that attract customers. The airplanes are better. It is people happy in their jobs, who satisfy customers when they come in. In the airline business it is the safety record.
Some Canadians are still afraid to fly. The safety record is an important aspect in attracting those customers and producing those thoughts. This privatization will serve consumers and employees well and customers very well, indeed.

Mr. Speaker, responding briefly to the challenge of the Hon. Member-and I take the challenge seriously-he has asked what Crown corporation or what agency of the Government of Canada has been privatized where job loss has occurred. The Hon. Member must be living in a dream world. The fact of the matter is, CN Route was privatized to become Route Canada. It has closed its terminal in many communities across this country, in particular in Sydney, Nova Scotia. It has closed its entire operation, throwing 22 people out of employment. That is what it has done. So do not tell me that these privatization matters that you people are engaged with, along with the Air Canada privatization, will not result in job loss. We have ample evidence to suggest, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that that will occur.
The Hon. Member is smirking over there, but he knows only too well that places like Charlottetown, Sydney, Moncton, Fredericton, Stephenville and Corner Brook will have major lay-offs within the next fiscal year. If he does not have the guts to stand up in the House of Commons to-
And de Havilland fired hundreds of people.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus).

Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in the third reading debate on Bill C-129, an Act to sell out Air Canada.
I want to deal with a couple of matters, some of which my colleague who spoke just before me has touched on, in particular, the interrelationship between the privatization plans of this Government and its deregulation plans. It is acting in concert, and one is the natural extension of the other. We started with the Liberals before the last election floating the concept of deregulation in the air industry. Changes were put in place to ease the restrictions to allow carriers to get in and out of the business much more readily and to get in and out of routes much more readily, in and out in the sense of providing services to it.
When we speak of the evolving hub-and-spoke system that has been developed in Canada, much as it did in the United
July 14, 1988

States and much as we predicted, we are finding less competition, not more, as a result of deregulation.
We now have the two major airlines, Air Canada and Canadian Airlines, owning, directly or indirectly, small feeder services that will service the hub airports of Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, Vancouver, Thunder Bay, Winnipeg and what have you, and then transferring on to the major carriers.
My colleague made reference to the problems in his area about individuals who have to fly in order to obtain medical services. One of the things that we found during our hearings into deregulation, particularly when we talked to people in the smaller communities or in the communities that were in such a geographical location that they had to fly to hospital, was that you could not get the same kind of service on an Air Canada DC-9 as you could on a Canadian partner that seats 19 people. You are unable to get a wheelchair or a stretcher in to transport an ill individual to those communities.
Although it is not directly related to the privatization of Air Canada, it certainly is part and parcel of the approach and the end result of the privatization deregulation push in this Government.
Let me deal with the Act itself.
How come Canadian Airlines would prefer to take smoking off their flights?
They saw the writing on the wall. This Government did not have the guts at that point in time to send a directive to Air Canada saying that that is what they would like them to do.
Don't be silly.

It took a New Democratic Member of Parliament, who had the courage for years to plant the seeds about that issue and was able to get legislation passed in this House, and in the other House, to ban smoking on domestic flights. That is what it took. It was not the Government that moved; it was a New Democratic Member that moved.
Don't be silly.

Now that I have their attention, let me go into the suggestions that my colleagues have put forward in terms of changes to the Bill, suggestions which unfortunately were not accepted by this House, by this Government in particular, which would have made what we think is a very bad Bill, a very flawed Bill, a little bit better, at least in providing some protection to the taxpayers.
The one that I was most interested in was the limiting of foreign ownership in Air Canada. The Bill currently follows international trends or conditions that maximize by 25 per cent the ownership of any airline in Canada. That is similar to a provision in the United States.
Air Canada
I gather that during committee hearings the committee was warned that the American Government is now moving to increase the allowable percentage and, because of the trade deal, which calls for harmonization between our two countries, that in fact Canada would have to follow suit. So if the Americans go to 40 per cent ownership allowable for foreigners, Canada would have to do the same thing. It would apply directly to Air Canada.
We tried to change that. We were worried that we might have a situation where one of our two airlines, whether it is Canadian or Air Canada, becomes acquired in large part by an American carrier and we develop into a hub and spoke system that is based not in our Canadian cities, where the hubs are, but in some of the major U.S. cities, and we find Canadians having to travel south to Minneapolis or Washington or New York before they could move back into Canada to another point. This is something that Sir John A. Macdonald made sure would not happen to the rail system when he arranged for the financing and development of the CPR to keep this country together. He was concerned about the north-south movement when what he really wanted was an east-west movement to keep this country whole. I would encourage his descendants in the Tory Party to rethink perhaps what they are doing in that regard.
The other amendment was to try to put into fact what the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), in tabling the Bill, suggested was there, and that is to limit the actual share offering. As we know, the legislation is open-ended. It could allow-and in fact the Minister has stated that at some point it will allow-100 per cent of Air Canada's shares to be sold to the private sector, to private individuals.
Hear, hear!

I hear "hear, hear". I am not surprised that some of the Conservative government Members want to see the whole airline sold. Given the way the legislation has been written and the directive given by the Government to Air Canada to vote its majority 55 per cent share with whatever the wishes of that minority group are, maybe it is just as well that they went the whole route. It is a half-baked pie that we have here. We tried to put in the legislation the restriction that only 45 per cent of the shares be offered to the public.
Let me deal with the philosophical aspect of this matter. Why do New Democrats oppose the sale of this Crown corporation? Is it because we like to own things as governments? Some people think that that is how we operate. Or is it because there is a need in a country like Canada to give the elected representatives of the people a chance to influence trade and travel patterns within the country? Yes, we have regulations that provide some level of control on transportation companies, airlines, railway and trucking companies. But if you give up the other element in the equation that government policy initiatives be directed through a Crown corporation to

July 14, 1988
Air Canada
provide services to the far North or to ensure there is a cross subsidization between the very lucrative Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto triangle and some of the smaller outlying region, there is a need to say to the Board of Directors of Air Canada that the bottom line cannot be their only consideration. Service has to be there not only to the major centres, to which many business people travel, but also to the Thunder Bays, the Sault Ste. Maries, the Sudburys of Ontario and elsewhere. The test of public convenience and necessity, which was there prior to deregulation, required an airline by regulation to provide a certain level of service. Perhaps it is a service beyond the economic capabilities of the community. We have seen in northwestern Ontario Dryden which has lost its jet service, a service it had for a number of years, a service very important to the economy of that part of northwestern Ontario.
Brandon too.

It was a symbol of being part of the mainstream. It is down to NorOntAir, Air Ontario and a Canadian partner, the very small lines. Dryden does not feel the same kind of attachment it had before. My colleague reminds me that Brandon used to be on a route connecting through Thunder Bay which provided jet service which has been taken away.
There are some economic impacts that go beyond whether or not a company makes a profit. While obviously we do not want to see government corporations losing money, we think it makes sense to force them to make it their mandate to provide those kinds of services. Through deregulation and privatization we have lost the tools we once had to ensure there is that kind of service.
There is another area we were concerned about. Under a policy direction, Air Canada has certain responsibilities with respect to the Official Languages Act to ensure the appropriate mix of our two official languages across the country. There is concern that as a private sector company there would not be the same pressure or controls. We want to ensure that the Commissioner of Official Languages is able to continue the monitoring process and what is still our national airline will provide service in both languages that we have come to accept as appropriate.
My Party and those we represent are concerned about privatization. We see it being done not for sound economic reasons, but more to satisfy a certain philosophical approach that is represented by the Conservative Party.
Which is sound.

We have seen Air Canada allowed to operate more and more as a private sector company without the benefit of legislation. We have not as taxpayers had to provide any money to Air Canada for many, many years. It has been selfsufficient, which is the goal of any Crown corporation, as long as it continued to provide services. We know from the documents available that the share assets of Air Canada provided by the Government of Canada have not been drawn upon.
Money is available allowing Air Canada to refurbish its fleet. There are all sorts of exciting and innovative ways of acquiring equipment that are not capital intensive and could have been utilized to ensure that Air Canada was able to grow appropriately. Yes, it would have cost money, but it would have cost a lot less than eight or ten nuclear submarines.
It is important as a symbol that we have an airline that is ours, not some small group or an individual or two. Air Canada belongs to all of us, every taxpayer today, and those yet to be born. We are the owners. This great movement to privatize Air Canada is not giving it or selling it to the people, it is selling Air Canada to a select few, taking it out of the control of the many through their elected representatives and giving it to a small section of our population and to people outside of our country. I do not think that is right, Mr. Speaker. I do not think that is an appropriate policy direction for the Government of Canada to take. That is why I and my colleagues will be voting against this Bill as we did at second reading.
We attempted to make the changes in committee and at report stage to make the Bill a little better. None of the amendments were accepted, even though I think they were appropriate safeguards that even the government Members should have considered more seriously. I think, because changes were coming from the NDP, Tory Members say, "Whatever the NDP wants is wrong and we will ram the Bill through in any case". That is not the appropriate way to do things.
There are no guarantees for the workers, no collective agreement job security clause. The guarantee for maintenance bases is weak, and other employees such as ticket agents and aircrew are not included. Flight attendants, who traditionally have had a number of bases in Canada from which to work, are not protected. Air Canada is being privatized with an eye on the bottom line. Air Canada could easily say to those people who live in western and Atlantic Canada, "Sorry we are not making as much money this year as we would like to. We will have to centralize and you will have to locate in Toronto and Montreal. You will have to leave your home in Winnipeg or Vancouver because it is more cost efficient to have you coming out of the major hub". Then there is the possibility of greater and greater foreign control. You have a situation developing of a privately operated airport terminal in Toronto. What happens if the company involved in that becomes attached to one of the American companies? What are the ramifications?
It would be nice if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would phone us and tell us he has been elsewhere in his community, has spoken to the Governor General and will call an election so we can kill this Bill as well as the trade Bill. Then we can get rid of the Government that should not have been elected in the first place.

You are history.
July 14, 1988

I am not history. I am here for a long time. I want to thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, in listening to my comments. I am sure there will be some interesting questions or comments from my colleagues across the way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the doom and gloom, the spreading of fear, the attempt to make Canadians nervous about unreal situations is incredible. It goes on and on and it has no basis in knowledge and no basis in honesty.
The Hon. Member should know that to get an airline licence in Canada, a company must be Canadian-controlled. He is saying that all these foreigners will take over our airline. If he had read the Bill itself, the subject matter of this debate, he would know that those who are non-Canadians who own shares can never, no matter how many shares they own, control more than 25 per cent of Air Canada at any meeting and for any purpose. All of their shares have to be prorated in terms of voting power so that collectively they do not exceed 25 per cent. Seventy-five per cent of the votes, in perpetuity, remain in Canadian hands. That is what the Bill says.
How can the Hon. Member bring that bogyman out in this Chamber if he has read the Bill? I challenged the previous speaker to name a privatization that had led to job losses, and he came back with something called CN Route. I did not have time to respond.
CN Route was a subsidiary of a Crown corporation. The board of directors had to make a difficult decision: should it wind the company down and throw 3,000 people out on the street, or should it seek a buyer who can make it viable, who can provide work opportunities, instead of throwing 3,000 people out of work. That is what that was all about, it was about protecting Canadian jobs by finding a viable ownership to keep the company alive and healthy and to make it work.
Does this Hon. Member have any evidence of previous privatizations of this Government and this Parliament that have not led to better working conditions for employees and more employees, even hundreds more employees in the case of de Havilland, more customers, better service, better products and better situations for the free trade environment? That environment will produce hundreds of thousands of jobs for Canadians, and members of his Party keep filibustering it.
Every reputable economist in Canada, not the lackeys of a few labour union bosses, tells us that it is time to join the modern age. It is time to be productive. Canadians can and will compete, and given the opportunity of a market, there will be more jobs, there will be better jobs and there will be a higher standard of living for Canadians.
Canadians have watched this filibuster. They have seen the 19 dilatory motions occur in the month of June, 1988, and they
Air Canada
know about the half a million dollars a day it costs to operate this Chamber, which is going down the drain on the basis of this filibuster. The Opposition's popularity is dropping like a rock because they do not represent the aspirations of the Canadian people. They listen to half a dozen labour leaders, not labour union membership, of a few rich unions. Those labour union leaders drive Cadillacs and have a different view of the world.
It is time to get back to the grassroots and listen to the people on the street. They want a healthy Air Canada. They see an opportunity to participate in ownership. They see a healthier company down the road, and regarding this filibuster on this Bill, the nation would be better served if the debate would end and we could get on to other government business.

Mr. Speaker, filibuster? Give me a break. We have had three speakers on this very important Bill. I would not call that a filibuster. Certainly I do not have the impression that we dragged out report stage last week. We certainly did not drag out second reading debate.
Let us face it. It was the Government that did a one-day wonder in committee. Is that consultation with the Canadian public to find out whether the Canadian public is in support of or against this legislation? Transport 2000 was not given an opportunity to appear, nor were other groups.
The Government knows that it cannot sell this to the Canadian people, so it wants to ram it through. It has forgotten about the tradition of this place that provides that matters of major consequence should have public and parliamentary review.
The Hon. Member talked about de Havilland. That was a company which the Government of Canada had to take over years ago. It had to pour millions into it, and as soon as it started to make a profit, the Tory logic told the Government to sell it so that someone else could get the gravy. That is incredible.
The Hon. Member goes on about the trade deal and all of these reputable economists who say how great we will do. Let me remind the Hon. Member that those studies were based on a 75-cent dollar. Where is that dollar now? Where are those jobs now? How can we turn over our country to an economic situation which has already been changed and over which we have no further control? Once again, the Government is not prepared to take the necessary steps to ensure that Canada can compete properly.
