subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider delaying its decision to purchase a fleet of nuclear powered attack submarines until the Canadian people have judged the proposal in the forthcoming election.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to introduce my motion calling on the Government to delay its misguided decision to purchase a fleet of nuclear powered attack submarines until the Canadian people have debated and judged the proposal in the forthcoming election. The Government, I suggest, has no mandate to proceed with what it boasts is the single most expensive military expenditure in Canadian post-war history. Just like the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal, this foolhardy proposal was not even raised during the last election campaign.
Furthermore, most Canadians want to express their profound opposition to it at the ballot box. A recent public opinion poll commissioned by the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament found that by a margin of two to one Canadians disapprove of the Government's plan. Any Government, even a Conservative Government that claims to be sensitive to the needs and wants of Canadians must acknowledge one simple and telling fact: Canadians do not want these submarines.
I want to explore the many reasons underlying Canadians' opposition to this proposal because, fundamentally, this plan raises questions about how Canadians see the world, how we see Canada in the world, what kind of threats we feel, and how best to respond to those threats. I want to begin with what is perhaps the most critical question arising under the proposal, namely its implications for Canada's maritime strategy and Canadian sovereignty.
The Government claims these nuclear submarines are needed to defend our sovereignty in the Arctic. That argument is patently bogus. So much so that even the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) is using it less and less these days. In fact, the Minister recently revised the subs' main mission to "patrolling on Canada's east and west coasts".

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext: That is what it has always been.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
However, the Minister, only last Sunday evening on The Nation's Business, returned to his original premise, namely that they were to protect Arctic sovereignty.
Naval analysts on both sides of the Atlantic have exposed the ludicrousness of the Government's bravado in saying these subs are intended to assert and defend Canadian sovereignty in the North. The Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament, for example, recently declared:
To assert Arctic sovereignty with submarines that will seldom be in the Arctic is like being represented diplomatically by the invisible man.
Veterans Against Nuclear Arms added that:
Canadian submarines are not going to be wheeling around under ice like police cars picking up vagrants.
Invisible men in police cars roaming under the Arctic ice picking up vagrants, is that the Government's concept of asserting sovereignty in the North? Like many Canadians, Ross Campbell, a former Canadian ambassador to NATO and former Chairman of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, is not deluded by the Government's claim that the submarines are designed to defend Canadian sovereignty:
It is not at all clear why nuclear powered submarines are needed to do a surveillance job equally well done by a combination of fixed sensors and conventional subs.
Canadians are demanding to know why the Government is planning to spend billions and billions of dollars to monitor the presence of foreign submarines in or near our Arctic waters when other means of protection, as alluded to by Mr. Campbell, would better serve our sovereignty needs. Tom Pullen, a
July 14, 1988

Canadian authority on Arctic navigation, rightly points out that ice-breakers, which are visible, would be more effective than nuclear subs in asserting our sovereignty by making our presence known.
The real irony is that Canadian submarines would have to communicate with DND headquarters through a communications network which includes the U.S. and other Allied navies because only very low frequency signals can reach a submerged submarine, and the Canadian Navy lacks this capacity. It is difficult to understand how a fleet linked so closely to U.S. communications networks and operationally coordinated with other NATO navies can expect to assert our sovereignty in the Arctic unless our claims to those waters have already been recognized by other nations.
In other words, nuclear powered attack submarines will not solve our outstanding territorial dispute with the U.S. if diplomatic efforts do not. For that reason, the Government's proposal has been dismissed by Donald Kerr of the International Institute for Strategic Studies in England and British naval analyst Anthony Preston as not a military program at all, but simply political posturing, and very expensive posturing to boot.
Canadians are also very concerned that the decision to Buy nuclear-powered submarines will fundamentally alter Canada's traditional defensive maritime strategy. As The Globe and Mail columnist Jeffrey Simpson aptly put it:
Make no mistake: the possession of these subs would represent a quantum change in Canada's strategic posture.
The Canadian Government has not given sufficient attention to the strategic implications of this plan, specifically as to how the fleet will be co-ordinated and, undoubtedly, integrated with the U.S. maritime strategy. Writing in the U.S. Naval Institute Proceedings, Ronald O'Rouke describes the U.S. maritime strategy as being characterized by "forward operation". According to Mr. O'Rouke, this involves:
-bottling up the Soviet Navy in its home waters-using one's forces offensively-particularly one's nuclear powered attack submarines.
He goes on to suggest that:
Only by operating in forward positions can the U.S. SSNs simultaneously perform these missions: help bottle up Soviet forces, threaten Soviet nuclear powered ballistic missile submarines and pose a tomahawk land-attack cruise missile threat.
Vice-Admiral John Anderson of the Canadian Armed Forces told members of the Standing Committee on National Defence on February 3 that in periods of tension, Canadian nuclear submarines could be sent to attack Soviet strategic subs. This admission confirmed the fears of many Canadians that these subs would be participating in the U.S. forward maritime strategy, including bottling up Soviet naval forces in their own waters. The acquisition of nuclear powered submarines will mean that Canada's maritime forces will be more, not less, subordinate to U.S. authority.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
False.
Nuclear Powered Submarines

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext: Admiral Robert Falls, ex-Chief of Defence Staff, has warned that any Canadian participation in the U.S. forward maritime strategy would be destabilizing inasmuch as it threatens Soviet missile carrying submarines directly and creates an incentive, as it were, for the missiles to be released before they are lost. Furthermore, it is important to remember that all of this would be taking place in waters far from Canada since no Soviet subs have actually been observed operating in or near Canadian waters.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext: False.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
I am deliberately quoting reputable experts and authorities in order to have my friends in the Conservative Party understand what they have been saying. Deputy Chief of Defence Staff, Vice-Admiral Brodeur, acknowledged this recently, namely that no Soviet subs have actually been observed operating in or near Canadian waters, when he said:
At the current time we do not have evidence that Soviet submarines are entering into the Canadian Arctic.
Given that there is no evidence of Soviet incursions, no proof that Soviet long-range cruise deployments are contemplated, and minimal probability of a pre-emptive attack, a nuclear submarine fleet seems an irresponsible and wholly unnecessary proposal.
Some of the best wisdom on this subject comes from an unlikely source, the Conservative Member for Nanaimo- Alberni (Mr. Schellenberg). In a letter to his constituents last year, the Hon. Member wrote, and I quote:
But if the subs are really meant to scare anyone, the threat is surely halfhearted. What would one of our new subs do if they came across a Russian or American sub in our waters? We are not going to risk confrontation with a superpower over an incident like that... Canada is not a superpower. The use of submarines as a policy instrument for the attainment of sovereignty simply commits us to playing the game by superpower rules ... and that may be the worst of both worlds. For we certainly don't have the muscle to make foreign policy with a big stick, and if we try to do so, we may well lose our influential voice as a moderate and sensible member of the international community.
Most Canadians, including some Conservative MPs, do not want membership in the nuclear submarine club. They do not want to see this country drawn into a provocative and hostile maritime strategy which membership in this exclusive club represents.
The Canadian people never gave the Government a mandate to adopt such a military posture so at variance with Canadian traditions, a posture which would serve only to deepen tension and suspicion between nations at a time when the world has witnessed a welcome thaw in East-West relations. Canadians do want to give an emphatic no to this proposal, and that is what this motion, when passed by this House, will enable them to do.
The Canadian Centre for Arms Control also points out that in every one of the three traditional tasks of Canadian maritime command, including sovereignty protection and the

July 14, 1988
Nuclear Powered Submarines
defence of North America, other options, quite apart from nuclear submarines, would be better suited to these specific needs.
The much touted under-ice capacity of nuclear submarines is unnecessary in peacetime since detection and reporting of incursions can be done at far less cost. It is unnecessary in wartime when the enemy threat would not come in the Arctic, as we all know, but in passages to the Atlantic which would be monitored at so-called "choke points".
Perhaps retired naval officer Douglas Maginley passed the definitive judgment on nuclear subs when he wrote in Policy Options earlier this year:
The nuclear-powered attack submarine has limited uses. It is, in fact, the mechanical equivalent of the great white shark. Its only function is to kill; to sink ships and other submarines. It cannot make use of the sea, only deny its use to others.
Canadians are also profoundly concerned about the threat these subs pose to our good international reputation and how their acquisition will undermine the nuclear non-proliferation regime.
Canada plans to declare that weapons-grade enriched uranium will be used for military purposes for these subs and then returned to civilian use. However, Canada would bar UN inspectors on the grounds that classified information might be obtained by Eastern bloc inspectors. Each submarine reactor will need between 150 and 200 kilograms of weapons-grade enriched uranium. This is a lot of material which is effectively being removed from international scrutiny.
While Canada is within its legal rights, as a signatory of the NPT, to take advantage of a loophole in the treaty, no other country in Canada's category has ever tried to exempt atomic fuels from international safeguards so as to use them for military purposes. In other words, Canada is the first nonnuclear weapons power to consider the use of nuclear materials for military purposes. In the eyes of many observers this would set a very disturbing precedent.
David Fischer, a councillor at the International Atomic Energy Agency, has said that Canada is imperiling its international reputation as a champion of non-proliferation by taking advantage of a loophole in the treaty.
It would also undermine the International Atomic Energy Agency's ability to reassure other countries that no uranium is being diverted which has, until now, been the foundation of the global strategy for curbing the spread of nuclear weapons.
Other signatories to the NPT could cite Canada as a precedent and also withdraw stockpiles of enriched uranium from public scrutiny. Perhaps more ominously, non-signatories to the treaty, on whom diplomatic pressure is continually brought to adhere to the treaty and the International Atomic Energy Agency's verification regime, including Brazil, India, Pakistan, and South Africa, could point to Canada as itself undermining both the treaty and the verification regime.
The Canadian Centre for Arms Control has condemned this aspect of the submarine purchase as a "major departure for Canadian policy and practice" which is "gutting an important arms control treaty".
The cost of compromising Canada's 40-year commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear materials could be immeasurable both in terms of our international reputation and global efforts to curb the spread of nuclear weapons.
Canadians are also profoundly concerned about the risks these nuclear subs pose to our delicate and precious environment. It is curious that the Department of National Defence, in answer to a written question of mine a few days ago, has just now initiated an environmental impact assessment on the proposed purchase. Who has been contracted to undertake the initial environment screening? Why, it is Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. I know a lot of environmentalists from across the country who would question the objectivity of an agency whose business is, in part, to promote atomic energy.
Canadians have reason to be concerned about the safety record of nuclear submarines. First, it is doubtful that Canada's claim to meet its exemplary standard for civilian reactor safety in the submarine project is even possible with the stingy budget proposed by National Defence to meet safety standards. More important, the past record of American and Soviet nuclear powered submarines is not a reassuring one, despite American claims that no accidents have been related to the power plant.
In fact, the loss of a U.S. submarine in 1963 was reactor-related according to the chief of the U.S. Navy's Bureau of Ships. Nuclear propelled submarines have run aground, sunk, and collided with warships, tankers, other subs, and even whales. A 1986 survey done by the Centre for Investigative Reporting in San Francisco revealed 99 incidents, 46 of which involved the nuclear power plant. At present, two U.S. and four Soviet subs lie abandoned on the ocean floor complete with nuclear reactors, certainly not very reassuring to all of us.
Also, the Department of National Defence has failed to outline procedures for decommissioning these nuclear submarines, particularly with regard to retrieval and disposal of all radioactive material and waste.
Perhaps it is appropriate to give the last word on safety to the father of the U.S. nuclear navy, Admiral Rickover. Late in life the Admiral became a vocal critic of both nuclear weapons and nuclear power. Before a U.S. congressional committee in 1982 he said:
I do not believe nuclear power is worth it if it creates radiation. Then you might ask me what I would do with these nuclear-powered ships-I would sink them all.
Finally I want to address briefly the incredible and still undetermined cost of this proposal. The Minister of National Defence says that Canadians can afford to foot the bill for this batch of nuclear subs. However, what he will not tell them is the precise cost of these subs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. July 14, 1988

Wilson) recently said that although the Government has some "general parameters" as to costs-whatever that means-it will likely be two years before an exact figure is available. What is clear, however, from all naval experts is that the basic cost of buying just the subs will far exceed the $8 billion figure the Government offers up as gospel.
The Canadian Business Council on National Issues has said $12 billion, Captain John Moore of Jane's Fighting Ships says $11.25 billion plus 50 per cent over 10 years for refitting, refueling and training, and the Canadian Centre for Arms Control says $14.8 billion.
A Conservative Member from Toronto is quoted in Maclean s as saying that "the cost of these things boggles the mind". Another Conservative Member from Quebec said in Maclean's this week that he is having a great deal of trouble explaining to his constituents why the Government is planning to spend all these billions of dollars on useless, provocative, unnecessary nuclear subs when the money could be spent elsewhere, as we all well know.
Surely Canadian taxpayers have a right to know the exact cost of this program before any decision is made to purchase this fleet. Finally, surely all Canadians have the right to debate and judge this proposal in the forthcoming election.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make some comments on the motion of the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) who proposes that we should defer action on the acquisition of nuclear powered submarines until after an election-type referendum. She is a little late. This decision was taken last year.
In the 1984 election, my Party made a particular issue of the sorry state of our military forces' equipment and our resolve, when elected, to implement corrective action. The unprecedented mandate we received in the 1984 election was, in part, an expression of approval for these military proposals. The people have already spoken.
Why nuclear powered attack submarines? The NDP is scandalized because these SSN's are attack submarines. There are no other kinds of submarines. Our Oberon submarines, those aging diesel electric boats, are categorized as SSKs, conventional attack submarines. There are no other kinds of submarines.
The NDP would appear to be oblivious that we have destroyers in our fleet and fighters in our air force. No doubt we will soon get an NDP motion to erase those naughty words from our vocabulary.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Why do you not talk about the U.S. forward maritime strategy?
Nuclear Powered Submarines

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Why submarines at all? I think it is worth spending a few moments reflecting on Canada's circumstances and Canada's needs.
The Hon. Member talks about the United States naval forward plan. We have no connection with that. It is not NATO policy. We belong to NATO, not the United States Navy.
We are a major trading nation. We depend heavily on the safe and timely delivery, by ship, of much of our trade. Our economic well-being, and consequently our social well-being depends on this secure sea trade. We front on three major oceans. We have the longest seacoast of any nation. Thus we have a vested interest, indeed vital interest in the safe and unimpeded use of the oceans, especially those that lap at our shores.
How do we achieve this? One way is in friendly and cooperative participation with other like-minded nations who share our views. Hence, we belong to various U.N. agencies and to NATO. We have a commitment, an obligation to those with whom we have made these commitments.
We have another obligation. That is an obligation to the nation of Canada and her people, our constituents. That obligation is to maintain those facilities and those forces necessary to patrol, protect, and exercise appropriate authority over these areas of land, air and water we call our own. No amount of weaseling around excuses any government for neglecting these basic obligations of office.
It would be very nice if we could declare the world burglar-free. Unhappily it is not. My own neighbourhood back home is not burglar-free. We find it necessary to maintain a police force and to encourage other organizations such as Neighbourhood Watch. Our oceans also have a variety of challenges awaiting us, from bogus refugees, to fish thieves, to drug runners, to potentially unfriendly naval forces camped on our doorstep.
We need in our inventory the capacity to deal effectively with all of these potential problems.
The NDP and Liberal defence critics have both publicly acknowledged that we require a Navy. So far, so good. They also agree with us that the Navy should be a mix of vehicles which include submarines. They also publicly acknowledge that nuclear powered submarines are the most useful and most cost-effective submarines we could have.
Having come this far on fact, evidence and logic, both opposition Parties now depart into the Land of Oz with all sorts of convolutions, contortions and distortions about cost, need and safety.
No doubt my Government colleagues will address the cost and safety issues. I limit my remarks to the need factor.
The NDP defence critic has suggested that the NDP, instead of building SSN's, would buy additional patrol frigates

July 14, 1988
Nuclear Powered Submarines
and up to 12 conventional submarines at a price some $2 billion more than our proposed expenditures.
Acquisition of conventional submarines would be a colossal waste of money. Even worse, it would be a dangerous and fraudulent waste of money. Such expenditure would try to delude the Canadian people that our defence needs are satisfied, and even worse would expose our submariners to a disastrously uneven contest in any conflict.
Given the military capacity of our potential adversary, we would be emulating the unhappy Polish cavalry who tried to halt the German Panzer divisions with horses and swords in 1939. That is the reality of the utility of conventional submarines.
The Canadian taxpayer, and certainly our long-suffering sailors, deserve capable equipment. The issue really is not should we or should we not have nuclear powered submarines. The real question is: Do we still need a Navy? The answer clearly is a resounding yes. Even the opposition defence critics agree.
We cannot afford quantity, even though our huge ocean expanses, our lengthy seashore, and our heavy dependence on ocean trade suggests we do indeed need quantity. The obvious route, the only sensible route, is to seek cost-effectiveness for what we do acquire. That means the SSN's.
The acquisition program upon which we have embarked calls for delivery of boat No. 1 in 1996, boat No. 2 in 1998, and one boat every 18 months thereafter until program completion in about the year 2010, which is 22 years from now.
There is an urgency to get on with the contract process because of the lengthy lead times required. We already face the prospect of a gap between the time when our three conventional submarines are scrapped for safety reasons and the time when the new boats come into service.
Thus we must get on with the task of replacement. The pending decision of country of source is still to be made, and we will need another two years of contract definition and contract allocation before commencing construction. We have lots of time between now and 1996 to change, amend, even cancel the program. What we do not have is time now to procrastinate. It may be the NDP's favourite policy on most subjects, but not ours. We see action as essential.
I look for an early decision and early action on this vital question of which submarine to buy. Whether to buy is long since decided.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATIONAL DEFENCE SUGGESTED DELAY IN ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in this debate brought forward by the New Democratic Party. The Canadian Government's intention to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, commonly known as SSN's, is entirely consistent with Canada's longstanding renunciation of both nuclear weapons for Canada and nuclear roles for the Canadian Armed Forces. These vessels
utilize nuclear power for the purposes of propulsion only. They will not carry nuclear weapons or nuclear explosive devices of any sort.
The principle of using nuclear power for propulsion is much the same as using nuclear power to generate hydro-electricity energy which is a common practice throughout Canada and the industrialized world. It is fully compatible with our commitment not to acquire nuclear weapons.
Because of its size, Canada has some unique problems and some unique responsibilities. We must keep certain vital sea lanes open in our three-ocean perspective. We must accept our role in defending sea lanes which are vital to western Europe and no one can deny the importance the Pacific Rim will play in the near future to our way of life. Even the New Democratic Party accepts the concept of the three-ocean perspective.
The submarines will not only be used in the Arctic, they will serve our entire territory, the Arctic, the Pacific and the Atlantic. During the previous Government, our entire Armed Forces were allowed to deteriorate to a level never seen. After World War II, we had the third largest Navy and proud officers and sailors serving our country. This Government has been able to give back some of the needed improvements.
The nuclear powered submarines will be the cornerstone of the new Navy. The SSN has unlimited underwater endurance when compared to the conventional submarine, which must spend at least 15 per cent of its time recharging on the surface. That alone should prove the necessity of the nuclear submarine. If one of our submarines was going from Halifax to Vancouver using the North West Passage, which is normally a two-week trip, an intruder would have to assume that he could come in contact with a Canadian submarine anywhere in our territory. One week a submarine could be in the Atlantic and two weeks later, having travelled under our Arctic water, could find itself on our Pacific coast. As for showing the flag, once in port, like any other submarine, they surface but once they leave port they again become invisible.
We have heard so much about the need to protect our own territory instead of letting other countries do so. I am quite sure that everyone is aware that Canada has the longest coastline in the world. I believe it is estimated at some 37,000 miles, so we can see the great advantage of the nuclear powered submarines. We must be able to control our waters in the three oceans, and the nuclear-powered submarine will do this.
Another benefit of the nuclear-powered submarine is that it will be less polluting. The cost of owning these submarines, as has been pointed out, is $300 million a year spread over 27 years. Its all very well to have a sign put up in the North West Passage saying, "Keep out. Canadian territory", but it is even better to have a big watchdog on a leash. There was an interesting letter published in the Citizen yesterday with respect to nuclear subs. It reads:
July 14, 1988

In today's navy, where speed, endurance and reliability are of the utmost importance, a diesel-electric boat does not meet the needs of our navy. They are slow, have low underwater endurance, cannot proceed through the North West Passage in summer even under ideal conditions and their diesels pollute the atmosphere with carbon dioxide, adding to the global warming.
Moreover, should an accident occur, the batteries containing in excess of 13,000 litres of sulphuric acid could spill into the sea, adding to the pollution already in our oceans. The salt water, when mixed with sulphuric acid, will produce the deadly phosegene gas which could kill the ship's crew.
Conversely, a nuclear submarine can operate in all three of our oceans and, for the first time, exercise our sovereignty anywhere along our lengthy coastline without limitations, with speed and efficiency, this would be done without the pollution of our seas or air above.
The U.S.S.R. has 400 submarines and commissions one every five weeks.
Canada does require nuclear boats. To quote commander of the Marine Command, Vice-Admiral Charles Thomas, "The issue is not the cost of owning nuclear submarines-it's the cost of owning a navy."

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think what I was commenting on more than anything else was the difficulty people are having explaining to their elected constituents the enormous costs and the changing use of this particular instrument. It is now recognized by many individuals who are experts in this field that we will not be able to enhance our Arctic sovereignty with nuclear-powered submarines. In all likelihood, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, mentioned these submarines will in fact be used in the Greenland-Iceland-Norway Gap along with other NATO forces to contain the Soviet fleet in the North and will also be used by the U.S. in the Northwest Pacific in its forward maritime strategy. It is a strategy designed to destabilize the balance of power and it is a strategy that is going to create an additional incentive or momentum in the arms race. It goes absolutely counter to the peace initiatives that have come about lately and to the traditional approach of Canada. The costs of this program are enormous and Canada would be well advised to stay far, far away from it by ending this program.
The cost of the submarines are enormous in terms of destabilizing the balance of power, undermining the arms and peace negotiations going on and undermining the nonproliferation treaty. One of the other interesting things we do not hear about from the other side of the House is the skewing of the national defence budget. There are many, many other branches in the Armed Forces which serve this country well, which have earned an international reputation, and over the next 25 years they are going to find their budgets very short. They are not going to wind up with the promotions, the additional staff and resources.
If I were involved in search and rescue and wanted an adequate number of flying hours, new equipment, new techniques and additional personnel to serve the people of this country, I would be very worried that my entire budget was going to be skewed by the submarine program. The peacekeeping forces, the anti-submarine warfare programs already in place, have been proven and tested over a period of time. This budget is going to harm the personnel in the Armed Forces, their families and the programs wherein they work hard to serve the people of Canada. Mark my words, the cost of this will cause an enormous amount of problems for those people.
In addition, it will erode Canadian sovereignty. The participation is clear. We are not going to attack the Americans under the Arctic ice in which their presence is clearly known. According to Armed Forces NDHQ, there is no

July 14, 1988
Nuclear Powered Submarines
information that there are Soviet submarines operating under there.
We do not have a communications system to communicate with those submarines. We will have to use the American very low frequency communications system. That speaks in an interesting way for a national armed forces whose primary problem with sovereignty in the Arctic is the American's attitude toward the Arctic archipelago.
With respect to the fuel supply, the Americans are uncertain that they will give a long-term enriched uranium fuel supply. We are now dependent for that fleet on the United States. There is no agreement in place for that to happen. We will either have to buy our fuel supply from the United States or manufacture our own, which will cost several hundreds of millions of dollars.
Not only will we be dependent upon the United States for the fuel to operate our ships, we will be dependent upon it to use its communications system to maintain contact with it. We will likely be operating in a subordinate position in its forward maritime strategy.
The political costs to the Conservatives are interesting. There is a clear understanding in the minds of Canadians that this program is irrational. The two issues which are likely to loom largest in the next election are nuclear submarines and free trade. I admit that free trade is grey for some people. They are not sure about the conflicting stories that they are hearing. However, when they are asked about the nuclear submarines, they are absolutely clear that it is a crazy undertaking. They know that there will be an erosion of other programs. Not just the National Defence budget will be skewed. The people in the Armed Forces today will be harmed by it. They know that programs such as old age pensions and health care as well as others will be competing with funds that are already earmarked for the submarine program.
There is talk of this program exceeding a cost of $16 billion, and that that $16 billion represents an enormous cost in lost opportunities in the country. It represents things that we could do.
This is a very unfortunate program. It is ill-conceived by a Government which has not done its homework. It is gradually coming to the realization, as statements by a number of Members of Parliament in written form to their constituents now acknowledge, that the Government cannot justify those costs. It cannot justify the program. It is not related to Arctic sovereignty.
There are many other ways to address the question of Arctic sovereignty, and addressing them more effectively and cost-effectively than by using nuclear submarines.
It is interesting to note that we cannot assess where those costs will come from. One individual, the Commander of Canada's Army, Lieutenant-General James Fox, delivered through members of his staff a curious comment of the Department's plans to acquire the 12 nuclear-powered
submarines at a cost of $8 billion. The General's staff argued, first, that the submarine acquisition will not have any effect on other defence expenditures. Then in a conflicting statement it was argued that Canada will be able to afford the subs because $6 billion of the $8 billion have already been identified in existing defence expenditures.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whose salary will be cut? Whose promotions will not take place? Whose resources will be cut? I am surprised that my colleague from the Esquimalt-Saanich area can stand in this House as a former member of the Armed Forces and watch his brothers and sisters in the rest of the Armed Forces be cut to the bone financially. I am convinced that the Government will be forced by the people to see the light and that it will drop this crazy program before the next election, or certainly suffer defeat.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get into my presentation I want to convey some intelligence from the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) in respect to the Maclean's magazine article which was referred to before. He tells me, Sir, that he was interviewed by the magazine and his point of view was, like mine and that of most Members on this side of the House, very positive. We believe that the Government is doing what is right in this acquisition program. But, for some reason or other, anything in a positive light, a positive vein, was neglected to be printed in the Maclean's article. Perhaps that gives Hon. Members some idea of the objectivity of that particular publication.
The motion before us today asks that the Government delay its submarine acquisition program until after the next election. It is my view that this matter was decided at the previous election. I remember standing on the shores of the Arctic Ocean in 1984 handing out leaflets which provided a description of the PC defence policy. The fact that I was elected, along with 210 of my colleagues on this side of the House, would seem to indicate to me that the PC defence policy found favour with the electorate of Canada.
At that time we promised to guard Canadian sovereignty on the land, in Canadian waters and in Canadian air space. We wanted to give our military the tools with which to do that job. We wanted to defend the northern parts of Canada which hitherto had been neglected. There was overwhelming support for this policy.
The NDP ideas of getting out of NATO and NORAD were rejected. The Liberal policy of allowing our military forces and military equipment to decay were rejected by the people of Canada. Not only at the time of the election but also about a year ago, at the time of the publication of the White Paper on national defence, that overwhelming support was again there.
If we ask ourselves the question, do we need a Navy, and answer that question in the affirmative, as just about everyone here would, then the next question becomes this: what should become the make-up of that Navy? What can do the best job for the money available?
July 14, 1988

The Liberals allowed over a period of years for our Navy to deteriorate. Virtually what we have left is a bunch of rust buckets. Really what we are doing is starting from scratch. We are in the process of acquiring a number of new vessels. We did not have one minesweeper in Canada. We are in the process of acquiring 12 new frigates. I guess, to give the Liberals credit, that acquisition program started under them. It is our proposal to buy some 10 to 12 nuclear propelled-not nuclear armed but nuclear propelled-submarines over about a 25-year period.
The Liberal plans, when we came in to office, although they had not been put into the process of implementation, were to acquire some 18 frigates, about six more than we are going to get. These things cost about half a billion dollars apiece. Frigates do not come cheap. They do not come in boxes of corn flakes.
The Liberals were also going to acquire a fleet of conventional submarines. The price-tag over the 25-year period would have been about $2 billion in excess of what we plan to spend. It would not have done anywhere near as good a job.
The former Liberal Defence Minister, the Hon. J. J. Blais, as quoted in a newspaper article yesterday, admitted that he was a supporter of the Conservative acquisition program, that nuclear-powered submarines were three times as effective as a destroyer, or three times as effective as a conventional diesel electric submarine.
The Oberon submarines that we have are old. They have to be replaced. They are dangerous and we cannot use them any more. We have to buy a new model.
Who in their right mind would go out in 1988 and buy a brand new Model T automobile? One would not do it. If one is going to buy a new automobile, then one is going to go and buy the latest model available, the most fuel efficient, et cetera. Diesel electric submarines when submerged have to use batteries. We have had described to us the environmental hazards of diesel electric and battery-operated submarines. They can only go for two hours at maximum speed while submerged. What chance is there of a diesel electric submarine catching a nuclear submarine or getting away from a nuclear submarine? There is no chance at all. We would be submitting submariners to inappropriate and great risks by putting them out to sea in times of potential hazards in Model-T submarines.
The nuclear-powered submarine's range under water, under the ice, is virtually unlimited. These days no other country buys diesel electric submarines. The United States has several hundred submarines and it has three diesel electrics left. They use them for target practice because the Soviet Union still has a few diesel electric submarines.
The U.S.S.R. has a much more ambitious nuclear submarine acquisition program than ourselves. One of the Members
Nuclear Powered Submarines
earlier pointed out that it is acquiring submarines at a rate of one every five weeks.
If we buy these submarines, as the Government proposes to do, we can have a three-ocean Navy instead of a two-ocean Navy. For most of the year our Arctic Ocean is covered with ice, and conventional submarines cannot be used under the ice. A conventional submarine has to surface to recharge its batteries.
Furthermore, we would be unable to move submarines from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean without going through the Panama Canal. "Please, Mr. Noriega, can we use the canal? We want to get a submarine from Halifax to Vancouver". Whereas, nuclear powered submarines can be moved through the North West Passage in our own territorial waters without having to ask any one's permission.
In the Arctic the nuclear-powered submarine is the only one capable of operating there. That is my backyard. My constituents as Canadian citizens want to be as well defended as Canadians who happen to live in Vancouver or Halifax on the Pacific or the Atlantic. I feel that they have a right to be properly defended. The first responsibility of Government is to provide for the collective defence. I cannot accept any policy where the first response to any invasion would be to abandon northern Canadians to the enemy.
If we do not have submarines, we will not stop nuclear submarines from being present in the Arctic. There will be nuclear submarines there. The question we have to ask ourselves is, do we only want American ones there, do we only want Soviet ones there, or do we also want Canadian submarines in the Arctic?
If we do not have them we are abandoning our defence. We are abandoning our sovereignty to the Americans. That is the policy of the NDP and the Liberals. They want to abandon the defence of northern Canada to the Americans and let them do what they want, and let us have no say in how that defence is to be conducted. That is not our position. Our position is that we are quite prepared to take on the responsibility that goes with an Arctic power of some measure.
The proposed acquisition program of the Government makes eminent sense to me. With it we will be able to protect Canadian sovereignty. We will be pulling our own weight in the defence of North America. The acquisitions will be cost effective. On an annual basis they will amount to 2 or 3 per cent of the defence budget. It will not disrupt in any way other military programs, as the NDP have stated. These vessels are the most effective available. The acquisition is in keeping with the wish of the Canadian public as expressed in the last election, and as I am sure will be confirmed at the next election.

Mr. Speaker, my special thanks to the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) who raised the point. To me, it is so

July 14, 1988
Air Canada
obvious that a decision of this kind which involves enormous costs and is probably one of the biggest Government expenditures ever ... and then all of a sudden, they tell us: That's our decision. It's based on the White Paper on National Defence and that is our policy. I can't deny that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) gave us some excellent arguments.

My esteemed colleague, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) who has sat on the Committee of National Defence with me, and the Hon. Member who introduced the motion, made some points, but so did the member of the New Democratic Party.

The important thing is, and it must be said here in the House, that we cannot go on believing that a country like Canada, whose mission in the world is to set an example .. . Does joining the big nuclear club set an example to the rest of the world, considering Canada's well-established reputation? We have a right to think about it. We have a right to consider very carefully and very attentively all the points made by the Hon. Member from Vancouver. What I fail to understand is the rush to make a decision on a matter of such vital importance, a matter that can make or break Canada's reputation. She said, as others have said in the past and will say in the future, that we are entitled to ask ourselves whether it is Canada's mission to do this.
Is it good for Canada to believe that we should spend between eight and sixteen billion dollars on what many in the United States see as a great adventure? A retired admiral of the U.S. fleet-I am not quoting pacifists-said that as far as he was concerned, he would sink them all if he had the impression that, and so forth. You can read what he said. Personally, I think Canada is on the wrong track. We are just as sincere as the Hon. Members who spoke earlier, but we fail to understand why a decision of this magnitude should not be debated at length in the House of Commons and put before the Canadian people when the Prime Minister, in his wisdom, decides to call the next election. This is an important decision. It is a decision that is vital to the future of Canada's youth. Does it always have to be bigger and better? That is what I keep wondering about national defence.
In concluding, I want to say that my Party is clearly committed to NATO. We believe in that institution, which does not prevent us from wondering how we could improve it. My Party believes in our membership in NORAD, which does not prevent us from thinking about it, just as my Party believed in the cruise missiles, and after thinking about it, we decided that enough was enough, and that is why we are now against the cruise missiles. Mr. Speaker-this will be my last comment, and I want to thank you for your patience- embarking on this great adventure would make Canada a different country from what it is now. Canada has a reputation that is known throughout the world. We know that is not how
Canada is perceived. Canadian men and women have a right to ask themselves whether that is the kind of national defence they want. Make no mistake: We firmly believe that we need the army, we firmly believe that we need the navy, but we don't believe ... I think we are at least as honest as all these people who would have us rush almost blindly into a decision of this magnitude.
Finally, I would like to thank the Hon. Member who raised the subject for this debate, because it is probably the only debate we will have.
It is probably the only time Parliament at the end of a term of government has had the chance to say: "Be careful. Is it really what you want?"
I conclude by thanking you for your patience, Speaker. If it is impossible to delay and if the House continues to sit, I wonder if my colleague and I should look into the possibility of having an urgent debate on this matter, so that more Members could participate and we can obtain more information from the Minister. The Minister is very confused. He was talking about security and sovereignty; now he is talking about the Atlantic and the Pacific. The sovereignty issue seems to be flying away and I think we should discuss it intelligently.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise on this third reading debate and to follow up on the committee hearings in which I played a part. I do so in the name of the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), the Hon. Member for Vegreville, Alberta. This Bill primarily affects Ontario and Saskatchewan, so it has a central Canadian element to it and a western Canadian element to it.
After third reading the Bill will give the federal Government the authority it requires to proceed with the agreement made with the Province of Saskatchewan and announced on the February 22 of this year. It really has two parts. The first part allows the assets of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and a provincial Crown corporation, Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, to be merged. The second part of the Bill deals with the privatization of the merged company over a period of seven years.
Bill C-121 provides for the transfer of the assets of Eldorado Nuclear Limited to a new company in return for securities. The articles of the new company, which will be incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act, will specify certain conditions the new company will be required to honour.
