First of all, certain provisions will be included to allow a large number of investors to purchase shares, while ensuring that the new company will remain in Canadian hands and under Canadian control.
Thus, non-resident shareholders or affiliated groups may not own more than 5 per cent of voting shares. At any meeting of shareholders, votes cast by non-residents may not exceed 20 per cent of voting rights. Similarly, no Canadian may own more than 25 per cent of the shares issued. Furthermore, the new company may not issue non-voting shares.
The articles of the new company will provide that the head office shall be located in Saskatoon. We feel it is important for senior management of the company to be close to the primary mining facilities.
The proceeds of the sale of the securities of the new company will be used by Eldorado to discharge its obligations, including the debt which is an obligation of the Government of Canada. It makes a contribution to reducing the debt load borne by the Government of Canada. The two-stage plan, the merger and the privatization of Eldorado and SMDC, was recommended by Eldorado's parent organization, the Canada Development Investment Corporation, as the best privatization opportunity for Eldorado. This recommendation followed three years of detailed and complex negotiations and preparations.
Those of us who served on the committee heard a lot of testimony about the various efforts made to sell the company and privatize it. On the basis of testimony before the committee clearly this was the preferred option in terms of Canadian taxpayers. Both CDIC and its financial advisers, Burns Fry Limited, have stated that the transaction was equitable and provided fair value for Eldorado's assets. Having listened to that testimony, Mr. Speaker, it was clear that it was not an easy situation to assess, and I think they deserve some credit for a job well done.
The best guarantee of jobs and job security for any company is for it to be a healthy, viable operation with financial stability, competitive advantages, and a secure market for its products. All these conditions apply with regard to this merger and privatization effort. There will be positive benefits in terms of better and more secure jobs similar to those which followed other privatization initiatives of this Government.
I bring to the attention of the House the success of de Havilland where hundreds more Canadians have jobs because we were able to sell the company to a much larger entity with a better marketing system. Our capacity to manufacture the Canadian product, the airplane itself, has produced increased market opportunities and increased opportunities for Canadians.
One issue that all Members accept as a serious and important responsibility is that the employees of any privatized corporation and the public at large be protected adequately. In April, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) announced new uranium mining regulations. These new regulations reflect this Government's commitment to the health and safety of workers and to the protection of the environment. In testimony before the legislative committee, the Atomic Energy Control Board made clear that the privatization of Eldorado would not affect the board's authority under the Atomic Energy Control Act. The new company will be subject to the same regulations concerning the health and safety of workers and the protection of the environment as any other private or public corporation. That is true of all privatization initiatives. They apply before the privatization and after the privatization.
It is clear that the transaction we are proposing through this legislation will not affect the regulatory framework that oversees the uranium industry. Exports of uranium and nuclear materials will continue to be controlled and monitored by the AECB and the Department of External Affairs in accordance with Canada's nuclear non-proliferation policy. Other Acts and regulations such as the Canada Labour Code will also continue to apply to the new company.
[ Translation]
The new company will operate existing dump sites under the statutory supervision of the Atomic Energy Control Board.
The federal Government remains committed to developing and contributing to a solution to the problem of management of existing waste. To this end, the declaration of intent provides for a shared-cost formula. Management and the full cost of management of new waste will be the responsibility of the new company, within the existing regulatory framework.
Furthermore, the Government will ensure that Eldorado, in addition to all its commitments to local communities, will meet its other obligations as well.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope other Members will speak briefly to this legislation which opens up new opportunities for Eldorado. The merger with SMDC will create a significantly stronger company with the resources, technology, and personnel to compete effectively in the global market. The free trade agreement with the United States opens markets to us. Increased efficiency and productivity will take us into global markets with more effectiveness. History tells us that every nation since the Second World War which has entered into agreements, small nations with large nations, has broken the dependency upon the larger nation. Through increased markets we will get increased productivity, increased competitiveness, and a better sense of being able to compete in global markets.
The wide distribution of shares and restrictions on the ownership of shares will give Canadians and employees of the



July 14, 1988

company a real and direct interest in the future of the company. That too follows through with previous privatizations. Employees are among the first and the fastest to take a share ownership position because they have believed in a company and had faith in it. I am sure it will be the same in this case as well.
These safeguards will also ensure that control will always remain firmly in Canadian hands. At the same time the operation of the current regulatory regimes will ensure that vital public interests such as health, safety, and environmental protection will continue unabated.
This agreement will benefit Canada and it will benefit Saskatchewan. It adds strength to Canada's uranium industry in a manner that will enable it to contribute more to the national economy and to Saskatchewan's economy and to maintain its world leadership in uranium production and technology. As with all the privatization efforts which the Government has undertaken since 1984, this legislation encompasses a pragmatic and sensitive approach to the public interest as well as the continuing interest of employees and the communities concerned.
I hope the House will move expeditiously this evening to complete third reading debate so that we can proceed to other important legislation.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not want to move too expeditiously to other legislation because this one is important as well. We have to spend a little time on it, but I can appreciate the sentiment of my friend, the Parliamentary Secretary. Certainly we are going to move very quickly on this Bill.
I appreciate having this opportunity to speak at third reading on the reorganization of Eldorado Nuclear Limited. While I find there are some problems with this privatization and the amalgamation with the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, we feel that generally the Bill should be approved. In light of that, I would like to outline a few of my concerns, that I have and I hope the Government will be addressing them.
On reviewing this Bill the legislative committee was very fortunate to hear witnesses who highlighted concerns on Eldorado's activities in the past and the possible consequences of this proposed merger with Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation.
We also discussed problems which could occur as a result of the privatization of these two companies. This will not necessarily be a smooth merger, but if both parties act in the best interests of their intentions, then I think it can work.
While the Liberals continue to support Bill C-121, I would like to comment on specific problems incurred in the production and marketing of uranium. That is where the basic problems lie. While they have been allowed to fester for some
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
time, there seems to be an acknowledgement by all parties to the merger that these problems exist. It seems that it has at least been stated that there is a willingness to deal with these problems.
My argument is that if privatization is to be the solution for the debt problems incurred by Eldorado, then Canadians must be assured of several things. First, they must be assured that there is an adequate regulatory framework to monitor this unique commodity, uranium. Second, they must be assured that there is a vigorous environmental assessment of any new projects undertaken by this merged company. Third, they must have the assurance that we have in place a time frame, financing, and competent management which will be accountable to the federal Government so that it will clean up disposal sites. Fourth, they must be assured that no municipalities will be left in limbo as a result of the termination of ongoing grants in lieu of taxes by this merger. While we want to help the uranium industry and these two companies, we have to be sure that we are not leaving problems with municipalities as a result of this merger and privatization. I will explain further what I mean by that later in my remarks.
I would like to elaborate on each of the four issues I have mentioned. With respect to the regulatory framework, it is the Atomic Energy Control Board which has been and will be responsible for ensuring that the activities of the new company are undertaken in a manner consistent with public safety, particularly with respect to protecting the environment from the release of radioactive material into the atmosphere.
Testimony of Dr. Terrence Downey, who did his Ph.D. dissertation on the uranium industry in Canada, emphasized by historical evidence the safety, environmental, health, and social problems which resulted from inadequate government supervision during the war years when Canada virtually lost control of its supply of uranium as a result of contracts with the United States. Furthermore, supplies of this radioactive material were bootlegged out of the company confines. The long-term ramifications of this activity is still evident today in the Malvern subdivision of Scarborough, Ontario. Soil in this area is still suffering from radioactive contamination. We have before us a precedent of what inattentiveness, bad business practices, and no consideration for the environment can mean. Even 40 years later, the City of Scarborough is still suffering from these ramifications.
It was not until full government ownership of Eldorado was in place that discipline was imposed on the production and marketing of uranium. Even so, the committee was informed of a whole host of environmental problems resulting from uranium mining and refining. In Port Hope, Ontario, the cost of cleaning up the low-level radioactive site was estimated to be from $265 million up to $735 million. That is a tremendous amount of money to clean up a site which has been like that for a considerable period of time, much to the chagrin of the people living in the immediate area. Yet it is still there, though it has not been there for as long as the polluted site in Scarborough, Ontario.

July 14, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
There is an alarming aspect to the obvious need for supervision and monitoring of a company which deals with this resource. In testimony from two sources, officials of the Atomic Energy Control Board and Dr. Elare who headed a thorough study of nuclear safety in Ontario, concern was expressed about the capability of this regulatory agency to carry out its responsibilities. The Atomic Energy Control Board is responsible for the regulation of atomic energy in Canada. Yet, we heard from Dr. Hare who headed a study on nuclear safety in Ontario and from the agency itself that there were doubts about this very agency's ability to carry out its responsibilities. To me, that is tremendously alarming, and I think it is alarming to all Canadians who know about this very grave problem.
In discussing the need for a 50 per cent increase in resources, the President of the Atomic Energy Control Board noted in testimony before the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources on May 11 of this year the following:
I have a feeling we are crippled. It takes longer to do the work, but we also cannot do it as much in depth as we would like to do it.
The President of the Atomic Energy Control Board is saying that his own organization is crippled by a lack of funds. He is saying that it takes much longer to do the work and that when they do the work, they cannot do it adequately because they are not properly financed. This is the agency that is supervising, monitoring, and controlling the nuclear industry in Canada. To hear a statement like that from its President is alarming, to say the least.
In testimony to the same committee, Dr. Hare responded to the suggestion of increasing the size of the board by saying:
Yes. I think perhaps my most crucial feeling about regulation in this whole business is that the Atomic Energy Control Board is too small. When I compare it with the regulatory bodies in other countries, I am amazed with what they do, but at the same time I do not think this can continue.
In addition to the testimony of the President of the Atomic Energy Control Board, the chairman of a committee investigating the nuclear industry in Ontario is saying that the Atomic Energy Control Board is too small and that he is amazed that it is doing as well as it is. These are two tremendous sources of information, both condemning the inattention to and ineffectiveness of this board because of the Government's lack of action and support.
Dr. Hare went on to tell committee members that out of five board members, two were ex officio. What is relevant to this debate on privatizing a uranium company was his suggestion that the Atomic Energy Control Board did not have the scope to make proper decisions.
This board which oversees our industry, in addition to everything else, does not have the scope to make proper decisions. Dr. Hare stated:
It is quite clear to me that in making its decisions the board ought to take into account far more broadly than it can do at the present time socioeconomic, radiological and environmental questions for which the board members themselves have very little skill. So in my report I recommend that
the size of the board be increased so as to make such broader representation possible.
That is a very valid recommendation. If the Government is trying to cut costs, then the Atomic Energy Control Board which supervises our very vital and controversial nuclear industry is not one of the areas in which the Government should be cutting costs.
Doctor Hare also noted that the Board should remain a technical regulator. He said:
What I am saying is that those technical regulations should have been made by a board that is competent around the table to consider more deeply the socio-economic, health and environmental questions which are the real stuff of this business. The technical questions are not usually in doubt; it is the non-technical matters that really have to be discussed in depth, and they have been inhibited from doing this. Moreover, it has been their policy to avoid this.
That is alarming. We have placed our complete confidence and faith in the Atomic Energy Control Board. It has been a very good agency, but it is under financed and does not have enough members. The members it has cannot deal with a lot of the questions with which they should be dealing. They are only dealing with technical matters and not with socio-economic, health and environmental questions as they should be, and as Dr. Hare's study stated.
We need some definite attention to these matters. While we are agreeing to the passage of this Bill, we want to set out that we are doing so mainly as a business framework. We agree that the AECB can have as much jurisdiction over a private company as we can, but we must point out that the AECB has not had control over the public company. With government support it has to zero in more on the concerns of the citizens of Canada with respect to nuclear energy.
With respect to some of the environmental matters, representatives from Newcastle, Ontario, gave us a very enlightening presentation on the problems which occur when a regulatory agency does not or cannot adequately control the disposal of low-level radioactive waste from a uranium mine. They told us, because they are in the Port Hope area, about the problems they have with the waste site in their area.
Eldorado Nuclear placed its waste management facility near Newcastle on a site of approximately 30 acres of land adjacent to Lake Ontario. In this area, which includes not only Newcastle, but Port Granby, Port Hope, and Welcome, Ontario, there is a total of 880,000 cubic metres of low-level radioactive waste.
As I mentioned earlier, the cost of cleaning up this dump site is estimated at up to $735 million. One cannot help but question why the AECB has not been successful in stabilizing and decommissioning this environmentally sensitive dump site. Why has this been allowed to continue on the banks of Lake Ontario? Of course that waste is going to spread. If erosion takes place on the banks of Lake Ontario, as it very well could, seepage and leeching into Lake Ontario is going to occur that
July 14, 1988

much sooner. It is expensive to correct, but the problem exists and the price is not too great when we consider the safety of citizens of this country, in particular those in the Province of Ontario.
Bill C-121 establishes financing for cleaning up existing waste. The first $2 million will be provided by the new company. The next $98 million will be split, with the new company providing twenty-three ninety-eighths and the Government of Canada providing the other seventy-five ninety-eights. Canada will pay any amount over $100 million. Use of the waste disposal site at Port Granby has been terminated as of June 30. Fortunately the AECB and the Government got the message, got together and decided that they were not going to use at least this dump site any more. That is long overdue.
What is alarming about all this is the fact that the Government has condoned this situation for four years. It has not recognized the seriousness of having a dump site like this one in a residential area so close to Lake Ontario.
With respect to this merger, while the financing agreement is in place, I am concerned that there is no time frame in place to complete the decommissioning of this low-level radioactive waste site. The Government is saying that it is going to leave it in a state of limbo, that it is not cleaning it up, and that it is not helping the residents of the area. We want action from the Government. It has to tell us when it is going to start decommissioning this site. Furthermore, responsibility for cleaning up the site will be in the hands of the federal Government. Speculating on the estimated cost of $75 million for stabilizing the dump site, the President of the AECB raised a serious problem. Once again I want to quote from his testimony in the legislative committee:
According to the agreement, Eldorado would have to pay 25 per cent of that $75 million up to a maximum of $25 million, with the remainder to be paid by the federal Government. According to the Atomic Energy Control Act, we can tell Eldorado to make changes or stabilize a site, but we cannot force the federal Government to pay its share.
That is the difficulty. The federal Government is delaying the cleaning up of this dump site, but it has to decide. It has to act now to clean up and decommission the site. He went on to say that he wondered whether this might not lead to outright refusal. Obviously the agency is very concerned about whether the Government is acting in good faith with respect to this dump site. The President of AECB went on to say:
From a legal standpoint, I do not think we have any problem with the company; I think that the problem would be between the company and the federal Government. That is one of the questions we are asking ourselves. Will there be problems of this nature every time we want to impose measures that might be very costly?
It is in the open and the Government has to respond. It has to lead the way, take the initiative, and clean up the dump site. Yet it has been silent, even in the face of testimony from its own agency.
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
We heard similar concerns about the delay in the clean-up process expressed by representatives of Newcastle and Port Granby. I urge the Government to give the Atomic Energy Control Board a specific time frame in which to stabilize and decommission this site. Furthermore, I would hope that there will be vigorous environmental assessments of future projects by the new company. It may also be necessary to have a field office with Atomic Energy Control Board staff located in Saskatchewan where a substantial amount of the uranium mining will be undertaken.
With respect to the previous obligations between Eldorado Nuclear and Blind River, Ontario, one of the communities which I said I hoped would not be jeopardized or left in an indefinite position as a result of the privatization, it is my understanding that the new company will honour the commitments made by Eldorado.
The Town of Blind River will be assured of the continuation of the $85,000 a year grant that Eldorado made in lieu of school taxes with which Blind River is paying off a mortgage on a community centre. In addition, there will be a continuation of the town's right to lease the golf course for $1 a year from Eldorado. The new company will also agree to assume responsibility for the erosion of the river which runs through the Eldorado property and affects the golf course.
I want to say how pleased I am that the Town of Blind River has been given these assurances. I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who worked very hard on behalf of his constituents in Blind River to attain this assurance. He sat with me on the legislative committee and questioned the witnesses. I believe that the success which has been achieved was largely through the Member for Algoma. I think he deserves congratulations for his work. Without this Member's persistence and true loyalty to his constituents, the new company may not have assumed the previous contractual obligations of Eldorado Nuclear.
The new company will be made up mainly of Canadian shareholders. The Act says that non-Canadian shareholders can own a maximum of 20 per cent of the shares. However, I read something very alarming in the Saskatoon Star Pheonix on July 8. It reported the statements of the new chairman of the new company. The article read:
A 20 per cent restriction on foreign ownership could be lifted if there is too much difficulty in selling enough shares to Canadians in what will be the world's largest uranium producer, says the newly-appointed chairman.
If that is starting already, Mr. Speaker, the Government's legislation will not mean anything. Many of us are giving our approval to this legislation on the basis that non-resident ownership in the new company dealing with our uranium resource, which is of tremendous concern to Canadians not only from an economic point of view but from a safety point of view, will be limited to 20 per cent and absolutely no more. The Bill is not yet even passed, and the chairman is saying that

July 14, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
non-resident ownership may increase beyond 20 per cent if they cannot sell enough shares to Canadians. That is terrible.
I know the chairman and find him to be a very serious and capable individual. I do not think he would say this unless he has spoken to the Government about this possibility. If the Government is playing games with this issue-and I have no reason to believe it is other than that from what I am reading-it is acting in bad faith. I hope the Government is not acting in bad faith and is not seriously considering increasing the level of non-resident ownership in this company.
To emphasize this, the chairman said:
This restriction can always be changed, and those levels will be looked at as we go into the future... careful consideration would be given to increasing the 20 per cent restriction currently in place on foreign investment.
I think it is awful for that even to be mentioned at this particular time. Through you, Mr. Speaker, and through this House I want to serve the Government with warning that if it or any Government attempts to increase the percentage of nonownership above 20 per cent in this new company, our Party will fight it as hard as we possibly can with every means at our disposal.
In the interim, there are problems yet to be solved with respect to low-level radioactive nuclear waste. There are uncertainties about what the actual financing picture was. I doubt very much whether the values placed on Eldorado Nuclear and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation are accurate. I think this was a political compromise between two Governments. However, that is for the future to tell us. I honestly do not think the figures were accurate but, on the other hand, at least the head office will be in Saskatoon. I wish the people of Saskatchewan well and I hope that this company will be successful.
I ask the Government to maintain all due diligence in monitoring this opposition and to strengthen the Atomic Energy Control Board, not only for the sake of this new company but for the whole of the nuclear industry in Canada.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the New Democratic Party opposed this Bill to privatize Eldorado Nuclear when it was brought forward in the House; we opposed it in the House. We attended the committee meetings, listened to the witnesses, and questioned the witnesses. Everything we heard from them confirmed for us even more clearly than when we first opposed the Bill how correct we were in opposing it.
I will deal briefly with some of the reasons for our opposition, beginning with the financial ones. Atomic Energy Control Board officials told us that as a result of the operations of this company there are, in the area of the Towns of Newcastle and Port Hope, hundreds of thousands of tonnes of low- level radioactive waste very near Lake Ontario. Unless major steps are taken to contain the waste and eventually remove it, it will
gradually move into Lake Ontario and pollute the water which is used by millions of people.
This happened when Eldorado was a Crown corporation owned by the people of Canada. We are now turning it over to private investors whose main purpose, quite understandably, will be to make a profit. We are turning it over to them without adequate control of their future operations, and the Government of Canada has committed the people of Canada to undertake almost entirely the cost of cleaning up that waste.
Let us look at the record of Denison Mines, a privately owned company in the nuclear business, owned by Stephen Roman. I recommend an interesting excerpt from a book being written about Stephen Roman and Denison Mines. It shows how that company deliberately and consistently breached the most elementary rules for protecting the environment and the workers in order to make greater profits.
Those are the kinds of concerns we have about privatizing this company. First, we believe that it is financially a bad deal for the people of Canada and a good deal for the new owners, particularly because of the environmental aspect.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) related the concerns expressed by the head of the Atomic Energy Control Board. I want to summarize the concerns of people living in the Towns of Newcastle and Port Hope and surrounding areas. They have not been reassured by this Bill. They have been expressing their concerns for years, which were essentially ignored by the former Government and the present Government.
They came to the committee with some specific requests, none of which were dealt with. They want a clean-up of the Port Granby dump and the continued presence of the federal Government in the disposition of the surrounding 650 acres where this low-level radio-active waste exists. They want an indication that a clean-up will proceed and that there will be sufficient funds to undertake it. Is there anything in the Bill that would give them that assurance? No.
Given the cost of between $250 million and $650 million to clean up this mess, there is nothing in the Bill nor in anything said by any government spokesperson to indicate that there are the resources or the will needed to finance the clean-up from the sale of shares, while the new company escapes with a very limited burden of some $25 million.
There is still no clean-up set for the Port Granby dump and other low-level radiation sites. This is not for good. This area has been campaigning locally on this issue at least since 1970. In 1984, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was Leader of the Opposition he promised a great deal more. Let me quote from the letter which the Prime Minister, then Leader of the Opposition, wrote to Mr. James Sculthorpe of Port Hope, Ontario, on August 21, 1984. He said, referring to the
July 14, 1988

activities of the Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence):
As Mr. Lawrence stated recently, there is ample evidence that neither of the current proposals by Eldorado Nuclear Limited for establishing a permanent radioactive waste disposal dump either near Port Granby or near Wesleyville are acceptable to the people of those communities or to their elected representatives. All such waste should be removed from major population areas and kept well away from any major water resource such as Lake Ontario.
While this would involve greater expense, the federal government, as owner of the Eldorado Nuclear Limited, must accept at least partial responsibility and provide the leadership.
For several years federal authorities have been exploring where and how to store permanently Canada's growing accumulation of nuclear and radio active waste. The waste from Eldorado Nuclear Limited must be considered part of that problem and its solution.
That was stated when the Prime Minister was Leader of the Opposition. All that was forgotten when he became Prime Minister. What we see is privatization, with no guarantees at all that the Government will do very much about the waste.
Let me deal with another concern expressed by the employees through their union. It is the question of pensions, which have become an issue in almost every privatization we have seen, including Teleglobe, Canadian Arsenals, and now Eldorado.
The Eldorado situation is supposed to be a very happy one, with a surplus of over $54 million in the pension fund. Many promises were made by the former Minister responsible for privatization, the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), and the President of Eldorado Nuclear, George Currie, that the surplus would be used to improve indexing and distribute other benefits to plan members. There was a statement by the then Minister in which she said that existing pension and benefit plans would be adopted by the new company. She went on to say: "I can confirm that pensions are protected by this agreement".
The President of Eldorado Nuclear gave the same assurances. Now we see that the Eldorado pension plan will be changed from a defined benefit to a money purchase plan and that such disbursements as indexing will be dropped. The current defined benefit plan, which could easily accommodate post retirement inflation protection for both current and future retirees will be dropped. Under the new money purchase plan, post retirement inflation protection for future retirees cannot be provided.
The surplus may be distributed by a contribution holiday which will reduce the surplus from $54 million to $12 million. Clearly United Steelworkers of America, representing the union members, was upset by this development as was made clear by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), in a statement which he made on July 7, 1988. He said, as reported at page 17236 of Hansard:
When the Government announced that it would be privatizing Eldorado Nuclear the Minister then in charge of privatization said in a press release that "existing pension and benefit plans will be adopted by the new company''. In a statement and a letter sent to employees she repeated that
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
promise. The company itself repeated that promise before a committee of the House of Commons.
Now in a proposal made public to the workers yesterday it becomes apparent for existing workers who continue to work for this firm that they will lose the protection of their present pension plans. The protection will only exist for those people who have already retired.
We see what the promises of the Conservative Government and the officials of the company mean.
Let me deal with another matter of tremendous importance. It is the question of job guarantees. We moved an amendment which was rejected by government Members, of course. It dealt with job guarantees due to the fears that the merger between Eldorado and the Saskatchewan Mining and Development Corporation would mean that jobs in the upgrading plants at Port Hope and Blind River would be in jeopardy. They are especially in jeopardy because of the free trade agreement which, according to Annex 902.5, exempts the U.S. from the Canadian uranium upgrading policy of 1985. Let me put that section of the agreement on record:
Export Measures
2.	Canada shall exempt the United States of America from the Canadian Uranium Upgrading Policy as announced by the Minister of State for Mines on October 18, 1985.
3.	The United States of America shall exempt Canada from the prohibition on the exportation of Alaskan oil under section 7(d) of the Export Administration Act of 1979, as amended, up to a maximum volume of 50,000 barrels per day on an average basis, subject to the condition that such oil be transported to Canada from a suitable location within the lower 48 states.
There you have, Mr. Speaker, another illustration of the serious adverse effects Canada will experience as a result of this free trade agreement. The testimony heard by the committee indicated just how the free trade agreement was part of a reshaping of the uranium market in North American which gives the United States access to our low-cost, high-grade uranium in northern Saskatchewan without the uranium having to be upgraded in Canada. This was confirmed by Professor Douglas McArthur, Professor of Economics at the University of Saskatchewan. He was questioned by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) about this matter and he said:
I think we are seeing an integration of particularly North American markets taking place, with free trade and other developments, the removal or virtual withdrawal from the further processing policy and so on. I am not very hopeful or optimistic for fuel processing in Canada under those conditions. Others will perhaps come back and tell you they are optimistic. I would challenge them to provide substantial evidence of this.
The Hon. Member for Algoma then asked:
Do you see the trade-off with the Americans and the free trade, where we are giving up our further processing, and they are doing away with the limitation on enrichment of Canadian uranium? It seems to me the administration has been fighting this, day in and year out, in the courts, and so on, to make sure they can buy $17-a-pound uranium from Saskatchewan anyway. If there were no free trade deal, are they not just going to pass a law that they can get access to this cheap uranium anyway? Did they just give us the sleeves out of their vest?

July 14, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
Professor McArthur answered:
I do not think there is a lot in that arrangement that is going to advance the interests of the Canadian uranium industry, I think it is going to have the result of making the various stages more competitive, which at one level is attractive. But it raises some serious questions, as I said, about the the future of Blind River and Port Hope. These are some of the consequences of moving into arrangements of this sort that one has to be aware of. This strikes me as being one place where we can expect to see some implications in terms of industry and cities and towns and people and workers in our country.
Those views expressed by Professor McArthur were never answered. They were ignored completely because, again, the Conservative Party has this blind belief that the private sector can do anything better than the public sector.
I would like to raise one other matter about which Professor McArthur spoke. He talked about how the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, a Crown corporation, made it a major tenet, a major reason for having a Crown corporation, that that corporation make every effort to provide employment for the people of northern Saskatchewan who are, in the main, native people. I do not have to tell Members of this House how disadvantaged, how poor and how sick native people are in many parts of Canada because there have been no jobs. The then New Democratic Government of Saskatchewan determined it would try to change that in northern Saskatchewan by using its Crown mining corporations to do everything they could to provide jobs for native people. They succeeded in that, and now what we see through the privatization of Eldorado and the privatization of Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, is a private corporation which will naturally have as its major objective, the making of profits. You can be certain, Mr. Speaker, that if it will be cheaper to employ people from southern parts of Canada, who are not native, then that is precisely what will happen. For these and other reasons with which I think my colleague, the Member from Regina, will deal, we intend to continue to oppose this Bill as we have from the day it was brought forward.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in the debate on Bill C-121, a Bill the Government has placed before us which creates a new corporation by combining the assets of Eldorado Nuclear with the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. When future historians look back at this particular period in the evolution of our society, I think they will view the action taken by the Government with Bill C-121 as one of the great and unfortunate mistakes of this particular period.
In the evolution of social societies, certain laws, which I cannot quite figure out yet, prevail and it becomes necessary at certain times to have right wing governments to correct mistakes from a previous period of evolution. The mistakes that right wing government makes in turn leads to its own defeat, and then society moves onward. Some people compare
it to the swing of a pendulum. It swings to the left and it swings to the right and somehow this produces social change and progress.
Bill C-121, I believe, will historically prove to be a tremendous excess of right wing philosophy. It is, as many Members have pointed out, an ideology defeating common sense. I would like to deal with this topic in terms of some of the sub topics. I would like to talk about the environmental impacts, the effects on the whole nuclear industry, and I would like to discuss some of the history of Eldorado. I would also like to discuss the business reasons behind this.
Let me take the last point first. Even from a business point of view, what the Government is doing today does not make business sense. It continues to astound me how a right wing Government that espouses business philosophy does at times make very stupid decisions. To put the assets of Eldorado Nuclear and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation on the market now just does not make any sense. The industry is in a slump. There is a surplus of uranium that has been stockpiled. It is not a good time now from a business point of view to dispose of the assets. It makes no sense whatsoever. Of course, the really dumb people are the Tories in Saskatchewan, the Government of Saskatchewan, because the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, from a business point of view, has indeed been a very successful corporation, bringing in revenues and royalties to the coffers of the Province of Saskatchewan on a very consistent basis.
I would like to quote from the paper presented to the committee by Professor Douglas McArthur of the University of Regina. He stated that over the four-year period since the company commenced production, and he was referring to the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, it has returned close to 50 per cent of the province equity excluding taxes and royalties. In its most recent year, 1987, the return on equity was 20 per cent, placing it well ahead of similar firms in the mining industry. Even though there is a slump in the uranium industry on a world-wide basis, the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation was able to show a return of 20 per cent on equity. That is certainly not the case when it comes to Eldorado. Eldorado had total cumulative losses by the end of 1986 of $155.9 million. Its cumulative return on shareholder equity over the period amounted to a negative 50 per cent.
Eldorado has some major and serious obligations, many of which in fact appear that with this legislation the Government will retain. For example, Professor McArthur in the paper he presented to the committee stated:
A second matter of concern has to deal with the handling of wastes and other potential liabilities contracted by the companies up to the time of the formation of the new firm.
The Government of Canada has indicated that there will be an effort to transfer to government (i.e. socialize) a considerable part of the responsibility for these to some degree unspecified liabilities. This suggests a curious ambivalence about the principle of privatization. Private ownership
July 14, 1988

generally implies obtaining the rights to the benefits of an undertaking, while at the same taking the responsibility for associated business obligations. In this case, the government intends to transfer the benefits to a select group of people with the ability to pay for shares, while imposing the burden of a major part of the obligations onto taxpayers in general. This is without doubt being done to enhance the marketability of the shares. But legislator and the public should be aware of the degree to which this compromises the principle of privatization, and the extent to which taxpayers are potentially burdened in order to meet a purely political, need with significant potential benefits for a select group of shareholders. Some have called this practice socialism for the few, which is a fairly apt description.
We see that this means does not make much business sense. I suggest that in Bill C-121 the Government shows that it is made up of lousy business people when it comes to conducting business for the public interest.
Let me reiterate. It is not a good time to put these assets on the market. There is a slump in the uranium industry. The Saskatchewan Government is made up of a bunch of damn fools for taking a very profitable operation and selling it off. It appears as though from a public point of view it is the public and the taxpayers of Canada who will be inheriting many of the liabilities from Eldorado. The new owners, the new shareholders, will not be acquiring those liabilities, which means the clean-up of soil that contains uranium wastes.
I would like to go back into the history of Eldorado to see why it was created in the first place as a public company. First, it was not due to a great amount of zeal for socialism by C. D. Howe that Eldorado was created as a public company. It became obvious that in the early 1940s during the war years the British Government was anxious to secure a reliable supply of uranium for its own joint effort with Canada to produce nuclear weapons. So, very quietly the federal Government of the day, a Liberal Government, started to acquire interests in this uranium mining company, Eldorado.
It thought that it had control over Eldorado. What it did is that it left the management of the company with a group that was initially there, a private group. By the end of 1943 the Government had acquired a controlling interest in the company, yet not a majority interest. However, in the spring of 1943 the British Government discovered to its dismay that Eldorado had contracted to sell to the United States all the uranium it could produce over the next two years. Despite the fact that the intention of the Canadian Government was to obtain a controlling interest in Eldorado so that it could meet its obligations to Great Britain, it left the management of the company in private hands.
These private managers did what good private managers do all over the world, managers who are mainly motivated by profit. They took the best bidder. The best bidder was the United States. All at once Canada was not able to fulfil its obligations to Great Britain.
When Eldorado was totally nationalized Mr. Grant Glasgow, a member of the firm of Clarkson Gordon, did a thorough review of Eldorado and its practices under private
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
management. It was found that, first, some of the top managers in Eldorado had sold uranium secretly. Second, it was discovered that there was some $2.6 million in cash and materials that had been extracted from the company. Third, it was discovered as well that practices that were detrimental both to the environment and to the health and safety of the workers were being undertaken. Those are the reasons why Eldorado became a public corporation.
Uranium is not just something that is dealt with like a commodity that can be bought at a cornerstore. What we are talking about is a substance whose negative effects will be felt for thousands and thousands of years. The effects of radiation, low-level radiation or high-level radiation, will be with us for generations to come. If you think, Mr. Speaker, of the time between now and the time of the construction of the pyramids, that time span is but just a twinkle in the time that the negative effects of radiation will be felt.
There are no social organizations, whether public or private, that I feel are responsible enough to deal with a substance whose effects will be felt for generations and generations to come. If I had my way, only a group of monks and nuns totally dedicated to the welfare and the well-being of the human race would be responsible for the uranium industry if we are going to have one at all. To hand it over into private hands is the ultimate of follies, the ultimate of stupidities, the ultimate of where ideology is master over the concern and the well-being of generations to come.
That is why at the beginning of my remarks I stated that Bill C-121, historically, will show to be the most stupid and inept act of this particular Government and the right-wing swing.
Let me put it on record that if I ever have in my power and am in a position of influence when this Government will be chucked out, as it will one day, then I suggest to all those who have invested in this new company that there will be many of us who will insist that this company be expropriated and brought back under public control without the type of compensation that they might otherwise expect. The uranium industry should not ever be in the hands of private industry. It is not an industry that works in a normal way. The effects are too long-term. It requires a sense of social responsibility to present and future generations that I suspect even publicly-owned corporations have a great difficulty demonstrating. To put it in the hands of the private sector that must show a profit on a yearly basis, and which is driven by market forces, is to invite disaster. It is irresponsible. The Government should be thoroughly ashamed of itself.
The Government states that there is nothing to worry about, and that it is going to put in place some regulations. In fact, it does not state that it will put into place some regulations. It states that the existing regulations will take care of the

July 14, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
environmental concerns, and the concerns for the health and safety of the workers.
First, let us recognize that the present regulatory regime was brought down under the assumption that there was a public Crown corporation in the uranium industry. I would suggest that the regulations need changing and updating to reflect this new reality.
This was definitely presented by Dr. Terrence J. Downey, Chairman, Department of Political Science, University of Waterloo, in a letter he wrote to the Clerk of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-121. He noted that the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) had invited him to send some of his observations to the committee dealing with the regulatory regime under privatization. In part, Dr. Downey's letter states:
In view of these considerations, I suggest that an enhanced regulatory regime must be put in place to correct current weaknesses and, of utmost importance, to bridge the major supervisory gap which will be created by a privatization which removes a key element of the regulatory framework.
In his letter Dr. Downey states that he has serious reservations that the existing regulatory regime is sufficient to ensure that this new corporation will be prevented from doing environmental damage and injury to the health of its workers.
Some very important work has been done on the effects of low-level radiation. We know from statistics that there was a tremendous increase in deaths from leukaemia throughout the world in the late 1940s and early 1950s as a result of the nuclear testing that the superpowers had been doing above ground. In fact, the statistics became so alarming that one of the first agreements on nuclear weaponry between the Soviet Union and the United States was to continue the testing underground because of the effect that low-level radiation was having on a global scale.
Some of the work now being done on low levels of radiation has shown a marked increase in deaths of those people born in the late 1940s and early 1950s in a period of time when there were high levels of low level radiation throughout the globe, and that there has been a marked increase in death and illness among that group of the population in the period of the Chernobyl disaster. The statistics now show that those people who were placed at risk because they were born in a time when there was a large amount of low-level radiation on a global scale were much more susceptible when the globe was in another period of massive low-level radiation because of the Chernobyl disaster. We see the effects of something that occurred 20 or 30 years ago later on down the road.
When we deal with uranium we must surely deal with it with a tremendous sense of responsibility and awe. By privatizing our uranium industry, I am afraid that we take a step away from responsibility. We allow it to be in the hands of people who are purely and totally motivated by market forces.
It is understandable when people invest in something that they expect a profit. They do not expect it in 10 or 20 years from now, they expect it at the end of the year. There is no doubt that decisions will be made that are primarily based on
the need to satisfy investors. That puts at risk the health and safety not only of the workers, but also of the environment, and generations to come. It puts at risk the health and wellbeing of the globe, the planet, and the children yet to be born, all in the name of some idiotic ideology of the Government and its insistence on privatizing, and that before the election it must have a good record of privatization. That is its motivation. Indeed, it is the height of irresponsibility. It shows and proves my contention that, at present, human institutions, whether they are government or private institutions, do not have the maturity and the responsibility of dealing with substances whose effects will be felt generations into the future.
Therefore, I must be opposed to this motion.

July 14, 1988

and did not complicate the situation through ownership. There is a normal, natural tendency among things that are closely interrelated to be influenced by other parts of that relationship.
I put this out generally as a difference of opinion, but I think that Government should restrict itself to setting down what the rules should be, making sure that there are adequate ways of policing the rules, and not complicating that any more than necessary with ownership, because the desire to please the ownership part of it might indeed complicate and make the world a little less safe.

Mr. Speaker, I have some trouble with that argument, particularly coming from this Conservative Member. We have heard from the Government over and over again that we must get government off its back and that we must rid of all these regulations. The mining industry hates government regulations. It is always at war with government because of mining regulations.
Now we hear a government Member justifying privatization of this industry. He obviously recognizes the need for a tremendous amount of social responsibility when dealing with nuclear substances and uranium substances. He says: "Oh, well, regulations will take care of that". I can see what will happen: "We will privatize it. We will have the regulations three or four years down the road. Well, there is another slump in the market. We will have to lay off workers. There are a few short cuts that we can make", and there go the regulations. We are getting government off its back, all right; I do not buy that argument!
I think he makes a valid point when he says that quite often public ownership and the regulators begin to come too close to each other. Yes, that is a danger and that is why we must have Parliament being ever vigilant to make certain that that does not occur. That is why we must always make certain that the representatives of the people-Parliament-has indeed the final say and that the wishes of Crown corporation become subservient to the wishes of Parliament.
To correct the possible danger of the regulators being too close to the Crown corporation, the solution is not to privatize. The solution is to make certain that the Ministry and Parliament are on top of the situation and ensure that that close relationship does not exist.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief in taking part in this debate. Our critic, our spokesperson for this Bill, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) has done an excellent job in putting forward the point of view of Liberals on this Bill and in putting forward possible amendments to improve the Bill. I cannot say that all our ideas were accepted, but I think one should recognize the excellent work done by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity, in the study of this Bill.
Certainly there is a point to be made for Bill C-l 10, since it rationalizes and combines three separate pieces of trade legislation into one. The rationalization and improvement of Canadian trade legislation is a central component of Liberal trade policy. This policy has been set out in the reports that we have put forward to the public. For example, the Liberal report entitled Reaching Out.
More precisely, we have said that in order to communicate effectively and to deliver federal trade policy it is necessary to have transparent omnibus trade legislation which addresses all possible trade issues.
I did want to put on record some problems that we see with the Government's approach. The Government has gone ahead and negotiated a trade deal with the United States. We have told the House and Canadian people how in our view the trade deal undermines Canadian sovereignty, puts at risk hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs, and limits the ability of present and future Canadian Governments, federal and provincial, to make decisions which Canadian people may consider in their interest and in the interest of their country in future years. I am talking about limiting the ability to make decisions in areas like energy, investment, financial institutions, agriculture, and cultural industries.
We now have a situation where the Government is trying to put us in a position where we will have two sets of trade legislation or rules. One set for our dealings with the United States and one set for everybody else. Ultimately I do not think that it will help Canadians or those who want to deal with Canadians, who want to understand and make the best use of Canadian trade legislation.
We have already made many comments about the flaws in the Government's trade deal with the United States when it comes to the rules set out in that deal on our trading relationship with that country. We pointed out that although the Government has set as its primary objective in a trade deal
with the United States the freeing of Canada from any possibility of harassment by American trade through penalty legislation.
It is very clear that we have not been freed from the threat of American trade legislation. Even if the trade deal becomes law, we will continue as before. The only difference will be that added to it will be another stage of bureaucracy, the so-called machinery which the Government says it has negotiated with the United States for a dispute settlement. However, this dispute settlement mechanism will do nothing other than decide whether or not the American law has been applied correctly according to its own terms. Also, there will be a very complicated set of rules arising out of the trade deal, if it ever becomes law, for determining whether goods can flow on a duty-free basis between Canada and the United States. Many Canadians had hoped that a comprehensive trade deal with the United States would mean that they could go to the U.S., buy anything they wanted and bring it back here duty-free. They are in for a big surprise, Mr. Speaker, if this deal goes through.
The rules provided in the Government's trade deal with the United States indicate that people who purchase goods in that country will still have to pay Canadian federal-provincial sales taxes. They will be able to bring in products duty-free, only if they can prove that those goods are essentially of an American origin. We know today that many of the things we want to buy when we go to a country such as the United States do not come from there at all but from countries like Japan, Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan. If that is the case, those purchases will be subject to duty as before. If the deal with the United States goes through, we will have one set of rules no less cumbersome than the rules that may exist at present dealing with our relations in trading matters with the United States, and another set of rules and a tribunal to examine the rules which will be set up under this Bill in respect of trade with all other parts of the world.
There is a second concern that I have to express about Bill C-l 10. It could well be argued that Bill C-l 10 does not cover a very essential area. The kind of trade legislation proposed by Liberals in the trade policy we have put forward would specify how complaints are to be processed and administered. However, this legislation will make it possible to deal with the issue of whether there should be federal assistance available to help Canadian industry that would be affected by any ruling of the tribunal to adjust to import competition. If so, what type and amount of assistance should be put into effect to bring about this kind of adjustment?
Bill C-l 10 does not do this. It basically prescribes how complaints and investigations are to be handled. An essential corollary of any ruling being made by the tribunal proposed under Bill C-l 10 is what effect it will have. If there are effects that will be evident because of a ruling, even though that ruling is said by the tribunal to be in the over-all Canadian
July 14, 1988

public interest, more attention has to be paid to the fact that this Bill is ready to allow the tribunal to help the affected industry adopt the machinery and technology to meet increased import competition effectively, or to enable the affected industry to move into other lines of production. It should also help the workers involved to get the skills and training which will enable them to keep their jobs in an industry which may be a very different kind of industry as a result of a ruling of the tribunal, or in some cases to help them go on to work in a totally different industry.
This key aspect of dealing with import competition has been virtually ignored by the Government's proposal. I hope that we will have the opportunity, and I predict another Liberal Government will have that opportunity, to do a better job than this Conservative Government has done until now, especially through Bill C-l 10 in addressing the vital issue of adjustment.
By way of conclusion I want to say that although I have brought forth some concerns about the Bill-and these concerns and others I have not mentioned have been expressed with a great deal of eloquence and insight by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity-I do want to say that our general position is that there is much desirable about Bill C-l 10 in so far as it rationalizes three separate pieces of trade legislation into one piece of trade legislation. As I have said, this kind of rationalization and the over-all improvement of our Canadian trade legislation are essential components of our Liberal trade policy.
I am glad to have put on record some comments on Bill C-110. I think we have reached the stage where this debate can be concluded, and for that reason I am happy to conclude my own remarks.
Mir. Ernie Epp (Thunder Bay-Nipigon): Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for a few moments in the debate on Bill C-l 10, an Act to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. I am tempted to say at the outset that this debate, brief as it will be, is a nice demonstration of why the House should not be sitting into July as it is doing now. This evening we are having a very brief third reading debate on a Bill that may be of enormous importance to Canadian industry, the manufacturing industry generally. It deserves to be treated with all the seriousness which that involves. Quite simply we have had persons from the Government, the Official Opposition, and my caucus speaking to the Bill who are not directly involved with it. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) is not here. I do not mean to violate the rules or cast any reflections at all, because his Parliamentary Secretary is standing in for him, but the Liberal House Leader and myself are here doing yeoman service for persons who know the Bill intimately, who are aware of its strengths and its weaknesses, and who would want, I am sure, to say more about it on third reading.
As the Liberal House Leader has done, I want to recognize the hard work of my colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), who worked very hard in
Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act
the House and in the legislative committee on Bill C-l 10. In fact, he had the satisfaction at report stage of having the Minister of State for Finance recognize the close attention that he had paid to this Bill and the work he had done trying to ensure that the Bill to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal would be an effective piece of legislation. May I say on his behalf, Mr. Speaker, in focusing my comments more particularly on the Bill, that in principle the proposal to roll together three different tribunals into one can be seen as a good thing. The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor would want to give his support in principle to putting these several bodies-The Tariff Board, the Textile and Clothing Board, and the Special Import Tribunal-together, to reorganizing them as the new Canadian International Trade Tribunal. That ought to be a good thing, but the question is whether in fact the Bill as it stands is a good thing, and whether the kinds of powers that have been assigned to this new tribunal, the composition of the tribunal, and the procedures that it is expected to follow in their individuality and totality would make an effective board. On behalf of my colleague and our caucus I want to say that we do not think it will be effective. We have very serious concerns about several aspects of the Bill and about the tribunal that it will create, if the Bill is finally passed, given Royal Assent, and proclaimed.
In my own observation one concern raised is the matter of easy access. The tribunal dealing with the textile and clothing board has been noted for its easy access. The textile and clothing board has existed to ensure that agreements dating back to the early 1960s in the clothing trade, which take the form these days of multi-fibre agreements with various Third World producing countries, and their impact on Canadian manufacturers are properly administered and that those industries are safe. The ease of access to the board has been one of its most important features.
Both textiles and apparel producers of Canada and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which speaks for far more of Canada's manufacturers, have expressed concern that the new tribunal will not provide this ease of access. One can see on the very face of it that with three tribunals and 15 members, even now the procedures are all too slow. If we move to a new structure with only nine members with far more responsibilities than the three different boards now existing have, there will be grave concerns about whether the new International Trade Tribunal will be able to work effectively and to respond to the concerns of industry as surely we would want that tribunal to do.
What makes this particularly ironic is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself, in a press release in Sherbrooke, Eastern Townships, the heart of some of Canada's most important textile and clothing producing areas, promised a greater role to the industry in shaping textile and apparel policy. Yet the legislation, Bill C-l 10, does away with a board which has played such an important part in studying the

July 14, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act
situation and making recommendations to government in the past.
Another serious problem that gives us cause to criticize and oppose the Bill is the matter of the discretionary power to conduct inquiries which the Textile and Clothing Board in particular has under Article 9 of the Textile and Clothing Board Act. That discretionary power is done away with in Bill C-110. In addition, the new reality is that the International Trade Tribunal will be prevented from making recommendations and reports on injury inquiries which would follow from the concerns of various industries affected by trade.
Given the particular fact that under the Act only producers who produce the majority of specified goods can petition for an injury inquiry, we feel grave concern for the small producers who are in a certain marginal position in an industry and who may manage in some industries, given the kind of price leadership which some are able to execute, to have a reasonably good life. Others may find themselves in boom time doing reasonably well, but when business is slow, they may find it very difficult to survive. In those circumstances particularly, will the small and marginal producers have any kind of recourse at all, given the way in which the International Trade Tribunal will be constituted under Bill C-l 10?
There is a third concern which relates to the question of an arm's length relationship which the tribunal is supposed to have with the Government. This is actually thrown into question by the fact that it cannot initiate its own inquiries. Does the fact that the large producers producing the majority of the products will have access to this tribunal make up for the fact that the tribunal is not able to initiate inquiries? The legislation is not very clear on this matter, but we can certainly imagine a situation in which the new tribunal will have a very close relationship with government and with large producers. What then is the situation of the smaller producers to whom I have already referred?
Since the purpose of this new International Trade Tribunal is supposed to be to deal with international trade and economic issues, it should surely have a much larger and more independent role in considering what is happening in the various industries, in initiating inquiries, and in recommending the kinds of adjustment assistance measures that may be necessary.
We are concerned that this Bill is surely part of the reorganization of Canada's trading system which this Conservative Government is carrying out. This is just one more example of the kind of bending over backward to U.S. interests which has characterized the Conservative Government in negotiating the trade deal that is being pursued these days in the legislative committee on Bill C-l30, and in other areas as well.
This is a Ministry which all too often has been ready to sell out to American interests, to forget what American industries do to Canadian industries, particularly through the use of American trade tribunals. In northwestern Ontario we have had to live for months with that 15 per cent export tax which
was imposed on Canadian softwood producers and continues to be imposed on Ontario softwood producers because this Government buckled under to American pressure. It was so stricken with fear that it would not be able to win before the American trade tribunal that it accepted an export tax on our lumber, though we in Ontario are convinced that there has never been any subsidization of the industry through stumpage prices for our timber.
If the Socred Government in British Columbia did not have the strength and courage to charge the proper amount for stumpage, then let British Columbia Governments go ahead and deal with the matter properly. We do not need American Governments under U.S. industry pressure forcing the B.C. Government to do the right thing. However, that should not be imposed on the people of Ontario, the workers in the forest and sawmills of Ontario, as it has been to the detriment of the industry and the loss of hundreds of jobs in northern Ontario already. In the context of what U.S. law allows and what U.S. tribunals make possible for U.S. industry, we see in this Bill just one more example of an inability of the Conservative Government to defend Canadian interests.
I note in glancing over the material my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor, has provided that he focused at report stage on a number of amendments which were designed to take care of some of these shortcomings in the Bill. Having read the record of that debate, I note that the Minister of State for Finance argued time after time that this would be some sort of a violation of our GATT obligations. He provided all kinds of assurances that all was well in the Bill.
We are not convinced of that. We are not impressed that this Bill will do things right. Because the amendments we put forward to try to make the Bill what it should be were not accepted, I state clearly now that the New Democratic caucus does not support Bill C-110, and when you put the question in a moment, Mr. Speaker, of course we will follow through on the statement I have just made.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few concerns about this legislation that I want to put on the record. I know that most Hon. Members would rather be at home than here this evening, so I will not take too long to say what I have to say.
Hear, hear!

I am sure that my remarks will be welcomed in the same enthusiastic fashion.
When it comes to the textile industry, there are theories of international trade, theories of free trade, and theories of prosperity coming as a result of greater liberalization of trade. When I put the theories of the economists on the one hand and the reality of the workers in the textile industry on the other hand, I find that my heart is with those in the textile industry. My heart is with those in the textile industry. I say that before we open our doors to greater competition in the textile industry, we ought to take care to see that the people presently
July 14, 1988

working in that industry will still have their jobs after these changes in legislation.
It is fine for a Prime Minister seeking an issue to run on in an election to hype free trade. It is well and good for economists who live in university ivory towers to promote the theory of free trade. However, when it comes down to the bread and butter issues for the people who work in the textile industry, they would like an orderly transition. They want their interests taken into account before legislation is changed.
We are afraid this legislation will weaken the instruments in the hands of the textile industry which ensure its survival. We in this Party have pointed out weaknesses in the legislation which ought to be corrected before it is passed. My colleague from Windsor introduced specific amendments because we want the people who work in the industry to feel secure and know that tomorrow morning, when they get up, their jobs will be there and that they will not be guinea pigs for some academic theory of free trade. Let us plan where we are going in an orderly fashion. Let us proceed with some care and caution. I urge the Government to accept the amendments we put forward so that the dangers contained in the legislation for the textile industry are not there when the legislation is passed.
It is well known that there are countries that produce textile products with labour which is paid at a much lower rate than is possible in Canada, even though the people who work in the industry in Canada earn low wages by our standards. Therefore, if we just throw open the doors to international competition, then we put the jobs of those presently in the industry at risk. If we are marching down the road to more liberalized trade, if we are going to bring down trade barriers, let us do it cautiously. Let us amend the legislation before it passes so the people in the industry will know that we have taken their interests into account and that we are not just following the theory of some academic economist or some political leader seeking an issue for a general election.
